#8353. The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

For nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks. Taken in 1909 and reproduced in books and journals, it showed Muztagh Tower as a vertical blade, a slender tooth of rock and ice rising from the glaciers with no obvious weakness. Generations of climbers studied it and concluded that the mountain was impossible to summit.

In the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems. But the photograph had misled them.

Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains. His uncle, Quintino Sella, had helped found the Club Alpino Italiano, and his father, Giuseppe Venanzio Sella, was a pioneer of early photography who published the first important Italian treatise on the subject.

Vittorio Sella combined serious alpinism with large-format photography. He made the first winter ascent of the Matterhorn in 1882, followed by the first winter traverse of Mont Blanc. Throughout his career, he carried heavy glass-plate cameras into the high Alps, the Caucasus, Alaska, the Ruwenzori, and the Karakoram.

Sella’s photographic technique was excellent. His plates were large, the detail exceptional, and the compositions carefully chosen. His work was much admired, including by American photographer Ansel Adams. In a 1946 article for the Sierra Club Bulletin, Adams paid tribute to Sella’s work, writing:

“The purity of Sella’s interpretations move the spectator to a religious awe. Sella has brought to us not only the facts and forms of far-off splendours of the world, but the essence of experience which finds a spiritual response in the inner recesses of our mind and heart.”

Vittorio Sella. Photo: Alpine Club Photo Library

Sella’s most important Himalayan photographs came from the 1909 K2 expedition led by Luigi Amedeo, Duke of the Abruzzi.

Filippo De Filippi’s official account of the expedition, Karakoram and Western Himalaya 1909 (published in English in 1912), was illustrated throughout with Sella’s images. Those photographs remain among the finest early records of the range. One of them, a telephoto view of Muztagh Tower, became famous far beyond the expedition report, and inadvertently sparked a legendary mountaineering myth.

Muztagh Tower (7,276m) is located in the Baltoro Muztagh of the Karakoram, on the border between Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan and China’s Xinjiang. It rises between the Baltoro and Sarpo Laggo Glaciers, just north of the main Baltoro corridor leading toward K2.

The peak has two summits only a short distance apart. The eastern peak is the true summit, and the western summit is a few metres lower. From most angles, the mountain is a substantial massif with steep but not uniformly vertical faces. From one particular viewpoint it collapses into something that looks far more extreme.

Muztagh Tower taken from the Upper Baltoro Glacier in 1919 by Vittorio Sella. The tower appears as an impregnable tooth. The photo inspired mountaineers for decades. Photo: Vittorio Sella

Sella took the image of Muztagh Tower from the upper Baltoro Glacier, looking northwest toward the mountain. The twin summits lined up almost perfectly. The long telephoto lens compressed the intervening ground and presented the peak as a narrow, knife-edged tower whose walls appeared to fall nearly vertically from summit to glacier.

From other angles the peak revealed broader ridges and less precipitous slopes, but this single compressed view was the one that circulated widely. The effect was really dramatic, but as later climbers discovered, also misleading. In 1941, Sella’s photo of Muztagh Tower appeared in a mountaineering book under the caption “The Last Citadel.” The image fixed the mountain’s reputation for decades.

Muztagh Tower, 1909. Photo: Vittorio Sella

In 1956, a British team and a French team both set out for Muztagh Tower, drawn in large part by Sella’s photograph.

The British team, led by John Hartog and consisting of Joe Brown, Ian McNaught-Davis, Tom Patey, and liaison officer Captain Riaz Mohammad, chose the Northwest Ridge. They planned to approach via the Muztagh and Chagaran glaciers on the western side of the peak.

The French party, led by Guido Magnone, included Andre Contamine, Paul Keller, Robert Paragot, Francois Florence, and liaison officer Ali Usman. They worked from the eastern side, aiming for what became the eastern arête after reconnaissance ruled out the North Ridge. The two groups operated independently on opposite flanks of the mountain.

The British established Base Camp on the Muztagh Glacier on May 28, 1956, at 4,282m. Through the first half of June, they placed camps on the Chagaran Glacier, avoiding the worst of the lower icefall by climbing the northern moraine and then threading seracs. Camp 3 was set on the west col at 6,355m after a steep ice wall. They reached the col on June 16, but took until the end of the month to move tents, fuel, and food up.

From there the route followed the exposed crest of the West Ridge, a mixed line of rock, snow and ice that required fixed ropes on the steeper sections. Brown made a key traverse around a rock cliff on the South Face. Camp 4 was placed on the ridge itself at 6,439m.

Above the high camp, the climbing continued up a narrow couloir and then mixed ground. The final technical obstacle was a short rock leaf between the two summits, graded alpine V and exposed on both sides.

On July 6, Brown and McNaught-Davis reached the western summit. The following day, Hartog and Patey, after supporting the first pair, crossed the connecting ridge and stood on the slightly higher eastern summit. Both pairs had to bivouac on the descent. Hartog suffered frostbitten toes. All four climbers reached the top.

Muztagh Tower. Photo: Hunza Adventure Tours

The French established their Base Camp at 4,496m on June 12 after approaching from the Younghusband Glacier. Their reconnaissance quickly showed the North Ridge was impossible, so they moved onto the eastern branch of the glacier.

They fixed ropes through an icefall and up a rock-and-ice spur, placing successive camps until Camp 4 stood at the foot of the summit pyramid at 6,300m. On July 6, as bad weather closed in, they spotted the British climbers moving on the upper heights.

After the two-day storm cleared, the French regained the ridge, overcame two substantial rock towers, and bivouacked high on the mountain. On July 12, Magnone, Paragot, Contamine, and Keller reached the main summit through deep snow, six days after the British first topped out. After summiting, they descended to Camp 4 after dark. Dr. Florence had waited at high camp for more than 40 hours without radio contact during the summit push.

The British party therefore made the first ascent of Muztagh Tower. The French completed an independent second ascent six days later. Both teams discovered that the mountain, while technically demanding and exposed, offered viable lines. The route, while serious, proved less relentlessly steep than Sella’s photograph had suggested.

The two expeditions were not engaged in a formal competition. They approached from opposite sides, followed separate routes, and maintained cordial relations. The British simply reached the summit first. The French, seeing the British already on top, continued their own line to completion.

Far from a bitter nationalistic race, the two teams demonstrated alpine solidarity. The French team chose the east side specifically to avoid interfering with British progress on the western side. Rather than abandoning their push in defeat after spotting the British on the summit, the French celebrated their colleagues’ historic achievement and resolutely pushed forward to fulfill their own objective. When Hartog suffered severe frostbite during his descent, the French team stepped in to provide vital assistance and support during the evacuation.

The southeast side of Muztagh Tower, showing the route. Photo: Guido Magnone for The Himalayan Journal

Since 1956, Muztagh Tower has remained one of the least visited major peaks in the Karakoram. A British team in 1984 repeated the Northwest Ridge (Mal Duff, Tony Brindle, Jon Tinker, and Sandy Allan), though they reached the slightly lower west summit rather than the true east summit. In 1990, a Swedish party consisting of Göran Kropp and Rafael Jensen also successfully scaled the Northwest Ridge.

In August 2008, Slovenian alpinists Pavle Kozjek and Dejan Miskovic made a groundbreaking alpine-style push up the steep Northeast Face. They successfully reached the upper ridge crest, but ferocious winds ended their push. Tragically, just after beginning their descent, a ridge cornice collapsed, and Kozjek fell to his death.

The 2,000m Northeast Spur of Muztagh Tower showing the line “Think Twice.” Photo: American Alpine Journal

Four years later, Russians Sergey Nilov, Dmitry Golovchenko, and Alexander Lange made the historic first ascent of the massive Northeast Spur. Their grueling 17-day climb via a new route named “Think Twice” reached the true summit, earning them the prestigious Piolets d’Or. The Russian team indicated in their expedition report that Muztagh Tower was 7,284m.

The 1956 French route has never been fully repeated to the main peak, and no further ascents of the true summit have been confirmed since the 2012 Russian expedition. Still, climbers continue to push limits here, most notably in 2019, with the first ascent of the Black Tooth (6,718m), a difficult lower spire on the mountain’s ridge.

Muztagh Tower (top left) and its Southeast Ridge, with a high point on the Black Tooth (6,719m). The solid line, with the two marked bivouac sites, is the line of ascent to Black Tooth followed by Simon Messner and Martin Sieberer in 2019. Photo: Simon Messner/American Alpine Journal

Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8352. Getting Rich Is Easy Compared To Finding And Keeping Love

As a parent, I have two main concerns for my children.

The first is economic stability. Will they be able to earn a livable wage in a world where AI keeps eating entry-level jobs? I question the time and money we spend educating our kids all the time. So I've been aggressively saving and investing for their future, just in case.

The second concern is bigger. Will my children find love?

A net worth target gets more achievable the more you save and the more time goes by. Compounding is boring, but it's reliable. If the direction is correct, sooner or later you will get there.

Finding a partner is far more amorphous. Our kids can work on their communication skills, fitness, charm, education, hygiene, empathy, and finances. But all of that merely improves their odds. There are no guarantees.

Which brings me to the strangest business story of 2026.

In late October, The New York Times reported that U.S. officials concluded a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a Chinese intelligence asset. She is a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and Nvidia cloud partner that rents computing power to Chinese firms.

Surveillance of her reportedly revealed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. And no, they are not related. Huang is a common surname like Smith.

The Financial Times then reported that a U.S. government memo described the relationship as romantic. Her alleged goal was to gather information on Jensen and advanced AI chips, and to nudge him to lobby for looser chip exports to China.

The allegations come from anonymous officials and haven't been tested publicly. Officials reportedly don't believe Jensen knew about any intelligence activity. Nvidia says his interactions with her were routine customer meetings. China denies the whole thing. House Republican committee chairs want a closed-door briefing on November 18.

So nobody outside the room knows the full story, except that Jensen admitted to the affair and is no longer CEO as of November 23, 2026. The lessons about love and money are worth discussing regardless of how the facts shake out.

Jensen Huang is worth over $120 billion (once $170 billion). He runs a company worth about $4 trillion after the sell-off. He is the closest thing we have to a modern-day emperor, the face of the AI revolution, mobbed like a rock star everywhere he goes in Taiwan.

And yet, if the reporting is accurate, it still wasn't enough.

There's a line from Gemma Teller Morrow in the TV show, Sons of Anarchy: “Only men need to be loved, sweetheart. Women need to be wanted.”

It's not entirely true. Everybody wants to be loved and desired to some degree. But the line points to something uncomfortable. No amount of money, applause, or leather jackets fills the need to feel admired by one specific person who seems to see you.

We all just want to be loved and accepted for who we are.

Here's the twist that makes this story sadder.

If U.S. officials are right, what may have felt like admiration was tradecraft. Attentiveness, respect, and flattery are exactly what an intelligence service would deploy against the most important man in AI. Intelligence services have used romance as an opening for as long as there have been secrets worth stealing.

Which exposes the hidden problem of extreme wealth and power. The richer you get, the harder it becomes to know whether anyone loves you for you. Every new person in your life has a reason to be nice to you. Normal people get to skip that existential headache.

Money doesn't make finding love easier. Past a certain point, it makes find true love harder.

The people worth keeping are the ones who liked you before you were worth liking.

Jensen is far from the first emperor to create a commotion over love for a woman.

Paris and Helen of Troy. The Greeks' foundational story is about a prince who ran off with another man's wife and got his entire city burned to the ground. Myth, sure. But the Greeks clearly understood the risk.

Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Antony controlled half the Roman world. He chose Cleopatra over Rome, lost at Actium in 31 BC, and both were dead within a year. Octavian got the empire.

King Edward VIII. In 1936, he abdicated the British throne after less than a year to marry Wallis Simpson, a twice-divorced American. He traded a kingdom for love, and spent the rest of his life in comfortable, irrelevant exile.

John Profumo. The closest parallel to the Jensen story. In 1963, Britain's Secretary of State for War was revealed to have had an affair with Christine Keeler, who was also involved with a Soviet naval attaché. Profumo lied to Parliament, resigned in disgrace, and the scandal helped bring down the government.

Brian Krzanich. Intel's CEO resigned in 2018 after a past consensual relationship with an employee came to light. Running a chip giant doesn't come with an exemption.

Jeff Bezos. His 2019 divorce after 25 years of marriage sent roughly 4% of Amazon, worth about $38 billion at the time, to MacKenzie Scott. Bezos kept his job, married Lauren Sánchez, and is still one of the richest men alive. But it was the most expensive breakup in history.

The pattern is clear. Kingdoms, careers, and fortunes are rebuildable. However, once you find the one, you will do anything to get them.

Remember Indecent Proposal from 1993? Robert Redford’s billionaire character offers a struggling couple, played by Demi Moore and Woody Harrelson, $1 million for one night with the wife. They take the deal. Their marriage nearly implodes.

The couple discovered they had a price, and it wasn’t that high. But they badly underestimated what they were selling.

Meanwhile, the billionaire could buy the night. He couldn’t buy her heart. He had everything except the one thing he actually wanted.

Swap Redford for any modern tech billionaire and the lesson holds. Money can buy almost anything. Except the feeling of being genuinely loved.

Plenty of regular people have become millionaires this way. The formula is public.

There is no formula for love. You can do everything right and still never meet the one. And even if you do, roughly 40% of first marriages in America end in divorce. Finding love involves tremendous luck. Keeping it is work.

You can always make another dollar. You can't always make another soulmate.

In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General declared loneliness an epidemic. About half of American adults report feeling lonely, and the health impact of social disconnection was compared to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.

The FIRE crowd isn't immune. Early retirement can be isolating. Your friends are at work. Your identity is gone. And if you're married, there's a specific trap worth sharing.

FIRE is better when both partners retire and experience freedom together. Not when one spouse is slaving away while the other is kicking back. Resentment will surely kick in.

Yes, I get it. Some men’s egos still need protecting when their wives are bringing home the sashimi. But men need to get over themselves. Women now make up the majority of college students, and plenty of them will out-earn their husbands.

I left banking in 2012. My wife kept working until 2015 when she negotiated her own severance. For almost three years, I was the guy at home while she commuted.

If you're planning FIRE, plan a joint exit. Life is better this way.

1) A high-value spouse may need more respect just to break even. If your partner is successful, attractive, or powerful, the world is constantly praising them. Next to all that adoration, treating them normally at home can inadvertently feel like a lack of respect, or even disrespect. So you may have to deliberately show more appreciation than feels natural just to run in place.

2) Everything gets taken for granted. Eat Kobe beef every day and you’ll get sick of it. In FIRE land, wake up without an alarm clock every day and you’ll take that for granted too. The antidote is voluntary discomfort. Scrub your own toilets after a big investment win. Take a part-time consulting gig a 40-minute bus ride away that makes you take orders from a micromanager. Practice fasting for at least 18 hours once a month if you have access to unlimited food. Doing uncomfortable things on purpose helps you appreciate the people you already have.

Whatever the full truth turns out to be, this whole situation is sad. Sad for Lori and their adult children. Sad for Jensen and his legacy. Disappointing for Nvidia’s tens of thousands of employees and shareholders like me. And a blow for America, given we’re in a global AI race.

Relationships are hard. They require constant work and attentiveness. Forty years of marriage doesn’t buy you immunity. If anything, it makes it easier to stop paying attention.

If there’s one silver lining, it’s that this story may help bring the left and the right together on maintaining our lead in AI. AI spending has been one of the biggest drivers of U.S. economic growth. If post-midterm infighting causes us to lose the race, we could sink the economy along with it.

If someone with that much money and goodwill was allegedly willing to risk throwing it away, you can’t really blame people for their emotions and their desire to be loved. We’re all human.

Besides a basic amount of financial security, I hope my kids will find someone who will support, love, and cherish them. I would rather my kids find that person than be rich.

Money can help protect them after I’m gone. But money can’t hug them after a bad day, sit with them in a hospital waiting room, or celebrate their wins with them. Knowing they each have someone like that is what will let me rest easy. That’s when I’ll know my kids will be OK.

Then I hope they never take that person for granted. Because the odds say they will, just like most of us take for granted the water we drink and the air we breathe.

Readers, do you agree that making money is easier than finding love? Would you take the $1 million in Indecent Proposal, or $2.2 million in today's dollars? If you've achieved FIRE, did you and your spouse exit together, or did one of you keep working, and how did that affect your relationship? And if you had $140+ billion, how would you ever know if someone loved you for you?

The distinction between financial stability and a lasting relationship is thought-provoking. Communication and empathy can grow with practice, but relationships also depend on choices both people make over time.

Forcing yourself to feel butterflies for just one person for fifty years goes against your genes.

Now we can survive without being tied to someone, yet our lifespans have doubled, and we still expect the same person to be our roommate, teammate, confidant, and lover.

#8351. Personal Investments • Re: How to incorporate an inheritance into retirement plan??

My DH and I are also likely to have some amount of inheritance. We chose, while working, to assume none. But that changed over the past 15 years, as everyone's investment accounts have grown beyond our models.

So how did we incorporate the potential inheritance?

1) We both retired at age 59. (We do have medical coverage as a retirement perk from my job).

2) We are front-loading some of our trip spending. Three trips/six weeks this year.

3) We are using some of our saved cash to accomplish Roth conversions before IRMAA is an issue.

That's as much as we were willing to push the assumption. If I were in your shoes, I would add:

- Move all of your current retirement savings to either a Roth or brokerage account. Pre-tax accounts are not something you will need more of, given the inheritance makeup and the 10 year dispersal rule.

#8350. Weekend Warm-Up: First Descent Rio Cuervo

This full-length adventure documentary follows kayaker Dane Jackson and a small team down Chile’s remote and wild Rio Cuervo.

With an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it. Dane Jackson launches into the complicated business of trip logistics, trying to find a way to get the team and their equipment to the beginning of the river. Besides him, the team consists of the trip’s mastermind, Kilian Astorga, and kayakers Tom Dolle, Eirik Hansen, Adrian Mattern, and David Sodomka.

Forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows. It’s gone now, so they turn to helicopter transport. With their gear dangling below on a rope, the chopper carries them up into the mountain, depositing kayaks and kayakers alike on the lakeshore. They set up camp and settle in to begin the first descent of the Rio Cuervo.

The team scouts the head of the river, swelled with recent rainfall. Photo: Screenshot

The dense forest and sometimes steep banks add another layer of difficulty as they begin to make their way downstream. They have to plan ahead, as there are stretches where it is impossible to bail if the rapids become too much. This means more portaging, which is painfully slow due to the thick vegetation.

When they do hit the rapids, on-board cameras capture the frenetic energy of whitewater kayaking. But the film makes no attempt to conceal the reality of a first descent. Much of their time is spent scouting ahead by drone, poring over satellite images, portaging, and standing about debating logistics.

Sunset arrives before the end of their portage. Camping in the jungle makes for an uncomfortable night. Photo: Screenshot

Jackson and the rest of the crew soldier on, though, cracking nerdy jokes (the jungle is compared to both Dagobah and Fangorn Forest) and making the best of bad weather and rough camping. In the final few days, conditions improve, and they can spend more time on the water.

The contrast between their slow, grueling push forward and the wild speed on the river brings refreshing energy to the kayaking sections. When the river finally widens as they glide into the sea, it feels like a hard-won victory.

Early in the production of a certain musical, Broadway director Harold Prince attempted to ask Andrew Lloyd Weber what the deeper political allegory or social commentary was behind the composer’s feline opus. Weber famously took a long pause and replied: “Hal, this is just about cats.”

This movie is about kayaking. Many outdoor adventure films use the genre, and the adventure story, to explore grand themes, and some do so successfully. But when they fall flat, is it more annoying than I can begin to express. For that reason, I deeply respect the clarity of purpose evinced by Dan Jackson and First Descent Rio Cuervo.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

#8349. Baselane Review: How to Stop Landlord Burnout From Costing You $800,000+

Rental property is how I broke free. The rent from my San Francisco properties was one of the foundations that let me leave banking in 2012 at age 34. Without it, I’d probably still be waking up at 5 am to get to the office by 5:45 am and leaving after 6 pm.

I’ve been a landlord since 2005. I’ve had good tenants, great tenants, and tenants who refused to take their trash with them during the final walkthrough.

I’m forever grateful for owning rental property. But the older I get, the less I enjoy being a landlord.

It’s not the math. It’s the tenant headaches, the turnover, and the maintenance. The 9 pm leaky faucet text. The final walkthrough that starts 30 minutes late. At 49 with two young kids, my time is worth more and my patience is worth less.

2025 tested me with three tenant turnovers. Each one meant a deposit to return, walls to paint, a vacancy to absorb, and a new tenant to find. Not long after, I sold one of my rentals. Earning 100% passive income feels better.

But selling also feels like giving up. Owning rental property is a war of attrition. The longer you hold, the more wealth you usually build. Hold until you pass, and your heirs may get a step-up in basis that wipes out the capital gains entirely.

Selling isn’t free either. Commissions, transfer taxes, capital gains, and depreciation recapture take a big bite. Then you lose the rent check and future appreciation on a property you’ll likely never buy back at the same price.

Semi-passive income you can live with beats optimized income you can’t wait to dump. You can’t automate away a difficult tenant or a burst pipe. But you can automate a lot of what surrounds them. That’s where Baselane comes in.

For 21 years, I’ve tracked my rental finances with a spreadsheet and emails. Old school. With three rentals left in San Francisco, it kind of works. I know my numbers, more or less.

But add another property, an LLC, a partner, or a short-term rental, and a DIY system starts to creak. Debits and credits slip through the cracks.

Four rentals is why I sold one last year. I couldn’t comfortably handle all the maintenance and management myself. And I didn’t want to pay a property manager 10% of rent or more to do a worse job than me.

Since Baselane is sponsoring this post, I opened a free account for one of my SF rentals to see how it compares. Here’s what stood out.

Baselane is a free business bank account, bookkeeping software, and rent collection app rolled into one login, built for landlords. Think business checking plus QuickBooks plus Venmo for rent, except it knows what a Schedule E is.

Banking and books live in the same system, so you never reconcile. Baselane is a fintech, not a bank. Deposits are held at Thread Bank, Member FDIC.

One of the first rules of landlording is to keep rental money separate from personal money. One of the second rules is that it gets messy fast once you own more than one property.

With Baselane, you can open unlimited checking and savings accounts under one login. One per property, one per LLC, one for reserves, however you actually run your portfolio. There are no monthly maintenance fees and no minimum balances, which matters once you're running a handful of accounts.

You can also issue physical and virtual debit cards with spending limits. If you pay contractors, cleaners, or a handyman, you can hand someone a card capped at, say, $1,500 for materials instead of fronting cash and chasing receipts.

The reserve accounts earn interest. Currently 2.88%. Letting a five-figure repair reserve sit in a checking account earning nothing is a donation to your bank.

If you try it, start with one property. Move its rent and its bills over, get comfortable, then decide about the rest.

Plenty of banks let you open separate accounts. What's different here is that every transaction gets tagged to a property and a Schedule E category as it happens.

Here's why that matters. Before my old Marina tenants moved in, I spent about $2,500 and many hours fixing up the yard. They agreed to hire a gardener twice a month. They never did. Before they moved out, I paid my landscaper $1,400 including materials to restore it, plus two days of my own labor.

Those are deductible repair and maintenance expenses. But only if you record them against the right property and can find the receipts a year later. With one property, I can do that myself. With five, it becomes a part-time job.

On the Smart plan, you set rules once, like “payments to my landscaper go to the SF rental under Repairs,” and an AI assistant handles the rest. You can snap a photo of a receipt and it matches it to the transaction.

This is the part that speaks to my real pain point: tenant headaches. It is also my favorite reason for using Baselane.

I rented my Marina house to five tenants from 2015 to 2017 for about $8,200 a month. The lease charged a $250 late fee after the 4th. Rent was late eight times in 24 months. I waived the fee every single time.

That’s $2,000 I left on the table because I’m a softie who dislikes confrontation. Their method of paying was walking into my bank branch and depositing directly into my account. One July 4th weekend, rent showed up on the 10th. That’s difficult to deal with when my mortgage is due by the 5th of each month, resulting in cash flow issues.

That awkwardness wore me down. In 2017, I sold the Marina house for about $2.75 million to simplify my life.

Thanks to the AI boom pushing San Francisco prices higher, that house is likely worth $800,000 to $1 million more today. Sure, I reinvested the proceeds, so the true opportunity cost is lower. But it still stings.

If I’d had a system to collect rent, send reminders, and enforce late fees without me playing bad cop, I would have held on. Selling out of fatigue can be one of the most expensive decisions a landlord makes.

That’s what Baselane does. Invoices, reminders, and late fees go out on schedule. Tenants can pay by ACH or card and set up autopay. Software doesn’t feel guilty enforcing a lease you both signed. Ultimately, Baselane removes friction which increases a rental property owner’s ability to hold on and build more wealth.

After 21 years, I've also learned that 99% of tenants want as little contact with their landlord as possible. The feeling is mutual. A system that runs rent in the background means fewer awkward conversations, and fewer awkward conversations means a happier landlord who's less tempted to sell.

Two catches. Tenants who pay by card pay a 3.49% fee, so steer them to ACH. And if your current rent collection works fine, then great. Baselane's value is rent, banking, and books living in one place.

If you run short-term rentals, payouts from Airbnb, Vrbo, or Booking.com can take several business days to clear at a normal bank. Across multiple listings, that's a constant gap between money earned and money available.

Baselane offers faster payouts when you use it as your deposit account on booking platforms, with each listing feeding its own account. Next-day payouts are available for free users.

A healthy bank balance doesn't mean a property is performing. You might have a big repair coming, insurance up 20%, or expenses sitting in the wrong account.

I recently ran the numbers on my San Francisco rental for a post on whether to raise the rent when tenants strike it rich. Rent is $10,250 a month, roughly $1,250 below market, because I honor a three-year rent schedule capped at about 3% a year. One vacant month wipes out about eight months of that discount. And a 2.5% annual increase only covers about 80% of my rising insurance and basic maintenance costs.

I know those numbers because I track them myself. Most landlords never sit down and run them.

Baselane builds income, expense, cash flow, and net operating income reports for each property or your whole portfolio, because every transaction is already tagged. No building spreadsheets from scratch.

With one rental and a spreadsheet you trust, you may not need this. With several properties or LLCs, it's the difference between knowing and guessing whether a property is worth keeping.

Tax season is where sloppy books come back to bite. You end up gathering records, digging up receipts, and trying to remember what a charge from eight months ago was for.

Because Baselane categorizes everything during the year, you can download a tax package with Schedule E reports, income statements, and transaction ledgers with receipts for each property and entity. Then you hand it to your CPA or use it to file yourself.

If you have one rental and a DIY system that works, you don't need it. But the Core plan is free, so there's little downside to trying it.

Baselane makes the most sense if you own several rentals, hold properties in LLCs, or self-manage. Property managers have quoted me fees ranging from 10% to 20% of rent. On a $10,250 rental, a 10% fee is $1,250 a month. Baselane Smart, its premium version is just $20.

That's not apples to apples. Baselane won't fix your garbage disposal or talk to your tenants. But if you self-manage, the administrative half of the job gets a lot lighter.

It's also worth a look if you're on the fence about selling a rental because you're worn out. Lighten the load before you list it and pay all those exorbitant fees. And if you're buying your next property, set up clean systems first. They're easier to build with one property than to retrofit with five.

Core is free and includes unlimited accounts, debit cards with spend controls, rent collection with automated reminders and late fees, property-level tracking, and the accountant tax package.

Smart is $20 a month with a 30-day free trial and adds AI auto-tagging, receipt matching, auto-transfers to maintain target balances, faster rent deposits, and balance sheet reports.

Compare that to what you may already pay. Some business bank accounts charge $5 to $25 a month in maintenance fees. At $15 a month across five accounts, that's $900 a year just to keep them open. Baselane charges no maintenance fees, no minimums, and ACH transfers and incoming wires are free.

No product is perfect, and pretending otherwise insults your intelligence.

Rental property helped me break free due to the semi-passive income it generates. But a rental only builds wealth if you can stand to keep owning it.

The headaches that make me want to sell are tenants, turnover, and maintenance. Baselane doesn't make those entirely disappear. What it does is take the money side of landlording, rent collection, late fees, accounts, and records, and put it on autopilot. Less friction overall means more energy for the parts that actually need a human.

My plan going forward is simple. Own fewer, better rentals and make each one as close to passive as possible. Let the private real estate side of my portfolio be 100% passive. And spend the time I save being a full-time dad.

If I’d had automated rent and late fees with my Marina tenants, I’d have $2,000 more and far fewer awkward conversations. I also might still own the house today. That’s at least an $800,000 lesson in letting small annoyances drive big decisions.

Selling a rental is permanent. Making one easier to own isn't.

If you own rental property and want it to feel a little more passive, check out Baselane here. The Core plan is free, so the only cost of trying it is an afternoon.

Have you ever sold a rental property because you were tired of managing it, not because the numbers stopped working? Do you regret it? What's the one landlord headache that would push you to sell: tenants, turnover, maintenance, or the paperwork? Do you track your rental finances yourself or hand them off? And have you ever waived a late fee you were fully entitled to collect?

What should real estate investors look for when choosing a bank? Look for property-specific accounts, integrated rent collection, automated bookkeeping, and tax prep support. Multi-property investors benefit most from platforms that organize transactions by property and entity automatically. Security deposit tracking also helps keep tenant funds clearly separated.

Can real estate investors open a business bank account online? Yes. Digital platforms like Baselane let you open accounts entirely online with no branch visit. Traditional banks may require in-person verification depending on their policies and your business structure.

Do any banking platforms for real estate investors offer high-yield savings? Digital-first platforms generally pay more on savings than traditional banks. Baselane pays a tiered APY on savings balances that exceeds the national average for business accounts. Traditional banks typically pay far less on business savings.

How do integrated banking and bookkeeping platforms help with taxes? Platforms like Baselane categorize transactions by property and IRS Schedule E category throughout the year. That cuts manual work at tax time and produces Schedule E reports and transaction ledgers you can hand to your accountant or use to file yourself.

Does Baselane support multiple properties? Yes. Baselane supports bookkeeping across multiple rental properties for U.S.-based entities, including single-member and multi-member LLCs, corporations, partnerships, and sole proprietorships. Banking and rent collection sync directly with bookkeeping, and you can connect external bank accounts and import historical transactions. See the pricing page for the full feature list.

What reports can real estate investors generate? Portfolio-level and property-level reports including net operating income, net cash flow, rent roll, tenant ledger, total inflows and outflows, transaction ledger with receipts, balance sheet, Schedule E, and income statement. Reports export for your accountant, lender, or tax filing.

#8346. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Lara Neumeier Makes First Female Ascent of a 5.14c: On October 7, Lara Neumeier made the first female ascent of Rhapsody (E11 7a/5.14c) at Dumbarton Rock, Scotland. She succeeded 20 years after Dave MacLeod established the route as the world’s first E11.

Neumeier’s ascent makes her the fifth woman to climb a 5.14c trad route. In an interview, she discussed the 15 climbing days and two visits spent working the route, how it compares to other routes, and her hope that the ascent will encourage more women to attempt the iconic line.

Karl Bushby, shortly after starting and now. Photo Facebook

I Left My 8-Year-Old Son Behind 28 Years Ago to Walk Around the World: After 28 years walking around the world, Karl Bushby should complete this Goliath Expedition within the next month. Now he faces an emotional homecoming: his son, whom he left behind at the age of eight, is now 36. Bushby has a grandchild he has never met, and his mother has seen him only three times since he left.

Julia Clarke hikes beside a stream in Mull, Scotland. Photo: Julia Clarke

Here are Nine British Hiking Rules Americans Need to Know: After returning to Scotland after more than a decade in Colorado, Julia Clarke realized she needed to rethink her mountain skills. She warns Americans not to underestimate the weather, terrain, or seemingly puny hills in Britain.

From wild camping rules and differences in hiking trails, to avoiding cows and brushing up on your navigational skills, she shares nine key differences American hikers should understand before tackling the British backcountry.

Women Across Diving Speak Out on Harassment: Women across the diving industry are speaking out about sexual harassment and assault. After years of raising concerns, petitioning and reporting to expedition operators and dive agencies with little outcome, many are taking to social media to share the experiences that have affected their careers as instructors, expedition leaders, and marine professionals.

Campaigners are demanding that the industry establish better and more accessible reporting systems, better safeguarding standards, and that operators vet their staff properly.

The Art of Progress: Climbing ethics are constantly evolving, and many are now reconsidering whether traditional ground-up ascents, minimal bolting, and preserving the original character of a route should take precedence over safety, accessibility, and the experience of future climbers.

Derek Franz explores this debate by looking at lines across Yosemite, Madagascar, Germany, and Patagonia, and the work underway to replace corroded bolts in many of them. The approach challenges the idea that a first ascent should remain untouched.

Three Dead After Avalanche in Chile: On October 17, an avalanche swept seven mountaineers into Laguna del Inca near Chile’s Ski Portillo resort. Three were killed and four injured.

The group was climbing toward Cerro Los Tres Hermanos when they triggered a slab avalanche. Rescue teams and the police responded within 10 minutes, and the survivors were airlifted to hospital. According to resort management, the group had entered a restricted area marked as an avalanche danger zone despite earlier warnings.

Old Traditions and New Developments on Mt. Kenya: Giovanni Trambaiolo explores Mount Kenya’s climbing history, especially the overlooked contributions of Kenyan climbers and the mountain’s deep spiritual significance to indigenous communities. He describes opening up Rainmaker, the new six-pitch trad route on the Temple Cliffs of Mount Kenya.

Three Mountain Emergencies in 14 Hours: Three hunting emergencies in northwest Colorado prompted search-and-rescue crews to respond within 14 hours, as the first significant snowfall of the season coincided with the opening of elk season on October 14 and 15.

Their first rescue call was for an overdue hunter, and the second from an individual who became separated from their group near Bears Ears and was too cold to walk. A third hunter suffered serious injuries when a tree fell on their tent as they slept. Another hunting party did not require rescue but got caught in snow, mud, and fog and spent over four hours finding their way back to camp.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

#8344. Couple Cycle America's New Golden Gravel Trail

Colorado couple Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle have cycled 6,124km along the newly opened Golden Gravel Trail. The Adventure Cycling Association created the route this year to celebrate its 50th anniversary.

The trail crosses eight states — Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Oregon — and stretches from Cape Girardeau on the banks of the Mississippi River to the small town of Port Orford on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.

Most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved. It is the organization’s longest off-road cycling trail, 1,120km longer than the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route.

The Golden Gravel Trail route. Photo: The Adventure Cycling Association

Stennes and Doyle finished in Cape Girardeau after 73 days, averaging an impressive 80km and around 12 hours of pedaling per day. “About 90% of it is mental,” they told Heartland News. “You might be tired, but you just keep on moving.”

The couple are both experienced long-distance cyclists who have previously finished Montana’s Big Sky Spectaculaire in six days and nine hours in 2022 (a self-supported 1,400km ultra-endurance race), among other bikepacking trips.

Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle during the 2022 Big Sky Spectaculaire. Photo: Bikepacking.com

Likewise, the Adventure Cycling Association suggests riders should be self-supported for the Golden Gravel Trail. Riders are advised to carry two or three days’ worth of food for the route’s most isolated sections, and up to a day’s worth of water. This is particularly important in the more arid sections, such as eastern Oregon. In Colorado, Utah, and Idaho, the trail traverses subranges of the Rockies and crosses the route’s highest point, Cumberland Pass at 3,668 m, in Colorado.

Stennes and Doyle say their journey included thunderstorms, aggressive farm dogs, and “countless hills.”

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8343. Just as the Rut Kicks Off, 2 Popular Climbing Stick Companies Issued Recalls

Published Nov 5, 2026 9:55 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Two hunting equipment manufacturers, Latitude Outdoors and Hunt Arsenal, have issued immediate stop-use notices following reports of potentially dangerous equipment failures. Both companies are investigating the reported issues and advising customers to discontinue use until further notice. Here’s what you need to know.

Latitude Outdoors has issued an immediate stop-use notice for its popular Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks after receiving reports of steps moving, slipping, or detaching from the climbing stick posts. This system of climbing sticks was popular among public-land hunters and even won our review of the best climbing sticks (before these safety concerns came to light).

A company representative says the company identified the bottom step as the point of failure after several customer complaints.

Latitude acquired Treestyx LLC in late 2025 and subsequently introduced the Carbon Synergy Climbing Stick. The product retained the original Treestyx design and construction while incorporating a new knotless attachment method.

According to Latitude, earlier versions of the product met industry testing requirements, and the Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks underwent additional testing and recertification before their release. Warranty claims involving the step-to-post connection have raised concerns about the product’s reliability, however, ultimately resulting in its recall.

Although the company said the reported failures represent a small percentage of products in use, it is advising all customers to stop using Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks immediately.

Latitude is offering full refunds to customers, regardless of where the climbing sticks were purchased. Customers who purchased directly through Latitude can initiate a return through the company’s online portal and receive a prepaid shipping label. Refunds are also available for Carbon Synergy Illuminators and Carbon Synergy Stealth Strip Kits purchased directly from Latitude.

Customers who purchased Carbon Synergy Climbing Sticks through authorized retailers should return them to the original retailer for a refund.

Retailers have also been instructed to discontinue sales and remove affected products from inventory. For more information, visit Latitude Outdoors’ return portal and see their official recall notice.

Obviously, this poses a major problem for deer hunters who are in the field now. Some social media commenters even claimed that they were going to take the risk and use the recalled sticks anyway, since they were already on their hunting trip.

Another popular saddle hunting company, Hunt Arsenal, has also issued an immediate stop-use notice for its 2026 Maxx Step Double and Triple Aiders. According to Hunt Arsenal, the attachment cord connecting the aider to the climbing stick may fray, separate or break during use, creating a serious fall hazard. The stop-use notice advises any customer using 2026 Maxx Step Double or Triple Aiders to stop using them immediately, even if the attachment cord appears undamaged.

While the company works on a solution, Hunt Arsenal advises customers to set affected products aside and not return or discard them until further instructions are provided. Hunt Arsenal expects to provide additional information early in the week of Nov. 9, including instructions for customers who purchased directly from the company or through authorized dealers. Hunters unsure whether their aider is a 2026 model should also discontinue use until they can confirm its production year.

The company said reports received so far involve only 2026 production models, and it is investigating a possible manufacturing issue that may have damaged the cord in some units. The Maxx Step Single Aider is not affected by the notice.

Updates will be available through Hunt Arsenal’s website and social media.

#8341. Climber Falls to Death on Ama Dablam

Search teams have found the body of Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, of Germany, who went missing after he reached Camp 3 on his way down from the summit. Evidence shows he fell 1,700m to his death.

Waschiczek was one among over 200 climbers who lined up toward the summit of Ama Dablam this past weekend. He reached the top on October 25 with guide Sonam Sherpa, but for some reason the two of them stopped descending at a rather high point on the mountain.

“The pair decided to stay at Camp 3 overnight after borrowing a sleeping bag and other gear from other climbers,” his expedition outfitter, Real Himalaya Nepal, told The Tourism Times.

Climbers above Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Dorjee Gyalzen Sherpa

According to the outfitter, the climbers prepared to continue down this morning. Lama asked his client to stay in place while he returned the sleeping bag to the tent where he had borrowed it. When the Sherpa returned, Waschiczek was nowhere to be found, but his crampons were still there, which suggested a freak fall. A search helicopter was called, and the remains of the climber were found this afternoon at around 4,500m.

Waschiczek is the first fatality on Ama Dablam this season.

Together with Manaslu, Ama Dablam is the most popular fall mountain in Nepal. The latest update from Nepal’s Department of Tourism on October 17 showed that over 300 foreign climbers had applied for a climbing permit. That day, the rope-fixing team opened the route to the top, and a massive summit wave started a couple of days later.

Virtually all foreign climbers are guided by one or two Sherpas, so the summit rates and numbers are remarkable. Local media estimate that over 200 climbers, among locals and foreigners, have topped out so far this season. Further teams should join them over the rest of October and November. However, no matter how tamed with ropes and anchors Ama Dablam gets, a fall from its steep slopes is usually lethal.

The upper part of Ama Dablam at sunset. Photo: 8K Expeditions

#8340. The 10 Best Rimfire Scopes of 2026: Budget to Precision Optics Tested

Published Nov 5, 2026 10:12 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A rimfire rifle used to be the next step up from a Red Ryder. You’d grab it to plink at the range, teach a new shooter, or shoot a few squirrels. But rimfire rifles have evolved, and so has the entire hobby of shooting them. It’s now completely normal to expect a rifle to shoot 1-inch groups at 100 yards and a range session to stretch from 25 to 300 yards.

Scopes have kept pace with the rifles. You might find a basic 3-9x on a stock 10/22, but you won’t find one on someone’s RimX build. Today’s rimfire shooter wants close-focusing adjustable parallax, a first-focal-plane reticle, and plenty of elevation travel to reach well beyond 100 yards.

I selected the best rimfire scopes with those demands in mind, but I haven’t forgotten the utilitarian and budget friendly scopes. Here are my top picks from my testing and our optics tests.

I use rimfires for hunting, fun shooting and occasionally competition. I’d typically need at least two scopes to cover those pastimes: a handy 3-9x for hunting and a 3-15x for shooting small targets at extended ranges. But the Nightforce NX6 2-12×42 F1 can take on all of those uses, and do them well.

We tested the entire NX6 line at Outdoor Life’s 2026 optics test, and I was thoroughly impressed with the 5-30x56mm F1’s ability to ring steel at 300 yards and focus down to 11 yards. That scope is a bit big for my typical rimfire uses. The 3-18x is a highly versatile option that Outdoor Life Editor-in-Chief, Alex Robinson, recently picked as the best high-end scope for deer hunting, but it’s still a bit heavy for my taste. The 2-12x is my pick for the ultimate rimfire scope because it’s ideally suited for small-game hunting, plinking and shooting steel beyond 100 yards. While it’s not the scope you want for hitting tiny targets at long range, it has enough magnification to hit rimfire-sized targets around 100 yards, and I routinely shoot my KYL rimfire rack with it at 50 yards.

The scope’s attributes extend beyond its versatility. It has decent glass, an incredibly easy-to-use zero stop, close focusing and excellent tracking. Some might find the FC-MRx reticle too busy, but I like it for fast holdovers and its reference points for wind holds.

I currently have the NX6 2-12×42 on a CZ 457 American with a Proof Research carbon-fiber barrel. The rifle is a hammer and very light, and the NX6 is right at home on it.

Read Next: CZ 457 American Review: Quarter-Inch Groups Right Off the Rack

If you’re looking for to compete in NRL22, there are several excellent scopes to choose from. But the Razor HD Gen III 6-36×56 is my overall best pick. It focuses down to 10 yards, has 36 MRAD of elevation adjustment, and plenty of magnification for shooting matchsticks and other tiny targets. The new VMR-5 reticle is a nice clean reticle that’s ideal for people who prefer dialing and you can still get the EBR-7 reticle if you prefer holdovers.

Here’s what optics editor, Andrew McKean, had to say about the Razor HD Gen III after our optics test:

Vortex might have been satisfied with simply upgrading the reticle inside its flagship precision scope, which has won enough PRS and NRL matches to qualify as a class leader. But with the new Gen III version of the venerable Razor HD, Vortex has created a new turret system that is precise, smart, and innovative.

The heart of the turret update is what Vortex calls its L-TEC+ zero system in which relaxing a single set screw allows users to make fast and precise turret adjustments. The system allows zeros to be established between the turrets’ .1 MRAD clicks, meaning that shooters no longer have to be satisfied with turrets set a half click above or below their true zero, a fudge factor that is more problematic the farther you shoot.

The operation takes a bit of getting used to. Tester John B. Snow, thinking the external slot on the head of the turret was designed to accept a beefy screwdriver bit, reefed on our sample, breaking the pot-metal, before reading the instructions and learning that once the retaining screw is loosened, the turret moves easily with only fingertip tension. Our other rifle-range revelation: The creepy caterpillar-looking grub that emerges from the base of the turret is not an embedded chrysalis but rather a smart revolution indicator that becomes fully emergent on the third full rotation of the elevation turret.

For the smart turret updates, the Vortex wins our Innovation Award, but that’s hardly the only update to this excellent scope. The new EBR-7D reticle is a marvel of efficient simplicity. Built around a .03 MRAD red-illuminated center dot with open aiming cross, the reticle’s elevation steps are in .2 MRAD hatches, and windage steps in .2 MRAD dots. We would like to see slightly bolder indexing, as the reticle references were hard to see below about 11-power.

The image delivered by the Razor HD is one of the best in the class, and we liked the turret indexing and smart and useful pull-to-turn illumination control. With a very close parallax adjustment and the infinitely adjustable zero, this would make an excellent rimfire competition scope.

Vortex is understandably proud of this scope, but with a retail price of around $4,000, we think it’s pretty pricey compared with its peer group. — Andrew McKean

There’s not much innovative or surprising here, just a basic duplex reticle inside a straight-ahead scope with decent turrets and a durable build. Backed by an excellent warranty.

If simplicity is the pathway to versatility, then the Vortex Crossfire II is at home on a small-game bolt rifle or a fast-shooting AR. It might not have the chops for precision work, but the duplex reticle is fast and reliable. The controls are a little mushy, but the eye relief and eye box are both forgiving and the fixed parallax makes it a great plinking scope. — Andrew McKean

Another in a long line of solid, bright Hawke scopes. This sub-$450 Vantage 30 is an upscale sibling to the Vortex Crossfire HD 6-18×50. Both sport useful second focal-plane BDC reticles with center-dot illumination. But the Hawke brings a little more sophistication to its controls, with exposed pull-to-turn turrets, immersive field of view, and a floating center-dot aiming point that lights up in either green or red.

Optics are good but not great. The illumination is good but we wish it was more intense to boost visibility in bright sunlight. And turret tracking started to slip a bit at the very end of its elevation travel.

But the Hawke impressed us with its smooth, tactile controls, and the BDC reticle is fast, with MOA-based references that correspond to the drop of standard center-fire loads. With a 50-yard zero with our standard 40-grain CCI .22 LR ammunition, we easily stretched the reticle to 300 yards by dialing 35 MOA of elevation and holding another 10 MOA. That’s impressive range for the scope-and-rimfire combo.

“It’s a simple, straightforward hunting scope that’s priced about right,” says tester Dale Manning. Enough said. — Andrew McKean

One of the surprises of the test is how testers universally fell in love with this little, versatile scope. On the surface, it seems like an oddball. Less than 10 inches long, it requires a cantilever mount to fit most rifle receivers, and it looks more like an LPVO than a serious precision scope.

But once you get behind the GPO Centuri Compact, a whole world is revealed through the excellent milling reticle. At lower magnifications with the illumination at its highest intensity, the reticle functions as a point-and-shoot red-dot sight. But at higher magnifications, starting about 10x, the reticle’s precision references become visible. A series of .1 MRAD hashes enables pinpoint aiming. For shooters who prefer to dial, the big exposed turrets pull to turn and move with authority. A smart revolution indicator pops up on the elevation turret when shooters enter the second revolution.

​If you’d rather tune the reticle to your specific load, GPO offers a free custom ballistic turret with purchase. That’s an additional value for a scope that’s already priced fairly at about $650.

Testers debated the best use cases for the Centuri Compact. Some felt it’s best suited to an AR carbine. Others wanted it on their big-woods whitetail rifle, and still others felt it would be an excellent scope for stalking elk in dark timber. That latter use is enabled with a smart illumination that lights up the floating center dot and inverted horseshoe. The red illumination is infinitely adjustable thanks to a rheostat control.

​The eyebox is stingy at higher magnifications, which forces shooters to have perfect alignment. But that’s a minor miss. The scope garnered enough pluses to finish in the top third of the field of scopes that are much more squarely configured for hunting.— Andrew McKean

The Busnell R7 won the editor’s choice award for being the best hunting scope of the year. While it’s an excellent big-game optic, it’s also right at home on a rimfire rifle. Here’s McKean’s take on this excellent piece of glass:

With this big, bright, and surprisingly sophisticated R7, Bushnell is restoring its relevance as a first-order hunting optic brand. The first focal-plane scope has an open tree-style reticle that’s anchored by an illuminated segmented circle and floating center dot that enables precision work as well as fast holdover and wind-informed shots at game.

For hunters and target shooters who would rather dial, the pull-to-turn elevation turret is nicely indexed and moves with positivity. The windage dial is capped.

Bushnell has invested heavily in the R7 line, which is the best of the Good/Better/Best product-line hierarchy that started with the R3 a couple years ago and continued with the R5 last year. The company has four different configurations of the R7, released just this month: a 1-8×24 LPVO, a 2-10×42, and a 3-15×50 in addition to the 4-20×50. The lower magnification scopes are available in second-plane reticles, but the two higher-mag versions come in either first- or second-plane reticles and either MIL or MOA, giving buyers a crazy number of variations on the platform.

We tested the second-plane MOA version of the 4-20×50, but for its versatility, performance on a wide range of targets and distances, and its flawless handling, we named the FFP R7 not only best Bushnell in the test, but the best overall hunting scope in the field of 25 excellent competitors. They include Nightforce’s new NX6, Leupold’s VX-4HD, and Zeiss’s new V3 families, along with some excellent submissions from Vortex, Trijicon, and Burris.

For its overall performance, the Bushnell R7 4-20×50 is this year’s Editor’s Choice winner as the top hunting scope of 2026.

The scope stacked points with a combination of good ED Prime glass, clear indexing on its controls, tight and positive turret and focus controls, and an illuminated Hybrid Dot Tree reticle that splits the difference between a precision competition and a hunting reticle. Its zero stop, which we’re glad to see on this type scope, is a 6-screw affair that’s a hassle to set, but works wonderfully as a solid backstop on elevation turret travel.

We worried about the durability of the R7, but it passed our inaugural drop test without skipping a beat. We dropped the scope three times from three feet on concrete covered by a 2-inch pad, and the Bushnell retained its zero.

Of course, our test teased out some deficiencies. The reticle references aren’t especially visible until about 7x, and I’d like to see one or two more intensity steps to the center-dot and segmented circle illumination to make them pop in daylight.

But if you’re looking for a rimfire or long-range competition scope that you can easily transition into a big-game hunt, this is a wonderful choice. The price, at about $950, is fair for the versatility and fine handling of this true crossover scope. — Andrew McKean

Set-it-and-forget-it hunters will appreciate this solid, honest scope for its lack of adornments. No illumination. A simple plex reticle in the second focal plane. It’s like the Fullfield mentioned above but with better glass and controls.

But hunters who are practiced at ranging a target, then dialing an aiming solution based on ballistic solvers will go crazy for this new configuration of the venerable Burris Veracity. The elevation knob is exposed, nicely indexed, and ready to dial. A little too ready, as it doesn’t lock. For some OL testers, that’s a problem, as an exposed turret can easily get pushed off zero given the hard knocks of the field.

But Burris has that figured out, too, with a zero stop that ensures a return to zero. It’s a tedious 6-screw affair to set, but once the zero stop is established, it is a rock-solid baseline for dialing.

​Given the wave of hunting scopes containing first-plane reticles with busy windage and elevation references and illumination modules, this iteration of the Veracity is refreshing. But it also forces users into either dialing for distance or sticking with the single aiming point at the crosshairs. We’d rather see the 3-15×44 Veracity with the illuminated RC-MOA (Rapid Cross) reticle that gives hunters the option of dialing or using reticle references to hold for elevation and wind.

We quibble a bit at the $1,000 price for such a stripped-down scope, but the turret tracking was among the best in the field, and Burris’s “Knob Synergy” elevation dial is tight, positive, and the low-profile build won’t hang up in the field. All in, the 3-15×44 version of the Veracity is a welcome addition to the 2.5-12×42 and 5-25×50 versions. — Andrew McKean

Combining simple controls and a modest but versatile magnification range, this durable scope is perfect for just about any .22 or .17, whether for small-game hunting, plinking, or most precision target work. It has good glass, repeatable controls, and enough holdover references on the vertical stadia that, with some practice, you can extend your range out to 100 yards and longer. At close to $300, it’s priced in the meaty middle of the market and can easily transition from a first-gun optic to just about any other rifle, whether a rimfire or not.

Here’s a rimfire scope for just about any purpose. This outwardly pedestrian optic has a lot going on between a surprisingly precise second-plane reticle, bright glass, and fun indexing on the nicely tactile turrets. The best thing you can say about any scope is that it is consistent, and the VX-Freedom delivers bullets with pleasing reliability. It’s a good rabbit and squirrel scope. Still, the MOA-based references on the vertical crosshair make it a decent option for engaging distant targets, which means you don’t have to invest in a ponderously big first-plane target scope to take titles at NRL22 competitions. Lastly, the Leupold rimfire scope brings the company’s good glass and an excellent warranty.— Andrew McKean

Tract’s 22 FIRE series has a full series of scopes for .22 and .17 shooters, but this AO model (it stands for Adjustable Objective) is the most versatile scope in the line from the direct-to-consumer brand. The duplex reticle features a fine crosshair with a .25 MOA center dot, which allows for full view of the target and precise bullet placement, which competitive bullseye target shooters will appreciate.

The adjustable objective enables precise focus for targets inside 10 yards all the way out to infinity, a feature you don’t often see on rimfire-specific scopes. The objective focus is a little clunky compared with the side parallax of most modern scopes, but it works well and further enables precise shooting. At about $275 it’s not a cheap scope, but the glass is good, the controls are some of the best in the business, and the precision it allows also makes it a killer squirrel scope. — Andrew McKean

The Burris Eliminator 6 is the easy button for long-range shooting. It ranges, calculates ballistics, and tells you where to aim. Here’s what shooting editor, John B. Snow, said about the Eliminator 6 in his precision scope buying guide:

This is the most innovative scope in this roundup. Burris has long been a category leader in scopes with integrated rangefinders, and Eliminator 6 is the newest iteration of that tech. Once the scope has been fed a ballistic profile and zeroed — neither process is overly complicated — it delivers impressive point-click-and-shoot capability.

The second focal plane reticle contains a multitude of LED illumination points. When you range your target — which is done via a large button on the left side of the scope or through a remote Bluetooth switch — one of those dots lights up indicating your hold. It is remarkably idiot-proof.

I know we live in an age of technological marvels, but the fact that you can roll through the scope’s magnification range and the aiming dot will slide up and down the crosshair continuously displaying the correct hold is remarkable.

Targets beyond 1,000 yards can become difficult to laze, and you’ll likely need to fine-tune your ballistic profile to keep the scope’s solutions spot-on. But within 800 yards this system couldn’t be quicker or easier to employ. — John B. Snow

Your first consideration if you’re in the market for a rimfire rifle scope is how well it will perform with the short-range capabilities of the caliber. You probably don’t need a ton of magnification or reticle references if all you want is to shoot tin cans or 50-meter bullseye targets. But the world of rimfire shooting is evolving to look a lot like long-distance center-fire precision shooting, with all sorts of precision rimfire competitions and games that put a premium on both short-range and long-range precision. For backyard plinkers, you probably just want a simple scope with a duplex reticle, but for the latter, you’re going to want a first-plane reticle with lots of turret adjustment. Then there are the pure small-game scopes. These are lower-magnification optics with just enough reticle references to get you on game and maybe make longer shots, head-shooting squirrels, for instance.

For small-game hunting, I want a scope that gets on target fast, has a reticle that “pops” from the background, but has enough references for me to place bullets precisely out to about 75 or 100 yards. In this collection, the standout hunting scope is Bushnell’s Trophy Quick Acquisition (QA), a 1-6×24 marvel that points quickly, has an illuminated center dot for low-light work, and enough holdover references for longer shots. Others worth a look: Vortex’s Crossfire II, and Tract’s 22 FIRE. At the other end of the spectrum is EOTECH’s expensive 1-10×24 Vudu, which doubles as a marvelous AR optic. Or consider Leupold’s VX-Freedom. Its simple duplex reticle is fast and reliable.

I like lower-power scopes for most rimfire work, whether that’s hunting or target shooting. A 2-7-power or even 1-8-power will give you all the magnification you need for most purposes. But if you’re interested in the precision rimfire competitions, then you’re going to want more magnification to really see the nuances of distant targets. For those times, I’d go with a 5-20-power or 4-16-power range, and make sure that precision target scopes also have manual focus—often called parallax—to bring targets of whatever distance into crisp focus.

The price of rimfire scopes ranges all the way from about $100 up to nearly $2,000. There are problems with both ends of that spectrum, just as there are great deals as long as you know what attributes you want and how you’ll use the scope. Starting at the lower end of the price spectrum, I’d be a little leery of super-cheap scopes, simply because they are probably made with substandard components and may not be as durable as higher-priced models. If you spend under $100 on a scope, make sure it has a good warranty that will cover any breakage or malfunctions. But you can buy a lot of scope for under $200. Scopes in this roundup include Bushnell’s Trophy QA and Vortex’s Crossfire II, and both the Leupold VX-Freedom and Tract’s 22 FIRE AO are both priced around $300 and offer excellent durability, utility, and warranties. Precision rimfire scopes can be especially expensive, largely because their precision controls and components are built to a higher standard. Still, the Sightmark Presidio, priced under $400, and the Vortex Strike Eagle are both worth looking at for budget precision options. On the other end of the spectrum, both the EOTECH Vudu and Blackhound Emerge offer tons of precision for rimfire shooters, but have all the attributes to transition once you move up to center-fire precision target shooting.

Somehow, the optics industry has squeezed all the fun out of rimfire shooting. Instead of cheap, reliable, and utilitarian rifles, we now have fancy chassis rifles with all the attributes of their big-bore brethren. And prices to match. We’ve complicated what was once the most fun and simple type of shooting into rigorous competition. That’s all great if you want to make .22 shooting into a serious thing, but don’t forget that rimfires are the gateway for most shooters and hunters into our community, and the scopes and rifles that are the best for new shooters are often the most simple and cheap. So read this review with a little bit of skepticism. There are optics for every stage in a shooter’s evolution, but maybe pay special attention to those fun, simple, gateway scopes.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8338. New Cyclone Approaches Nepal

For the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This new setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

The first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

Manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising

A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

The Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

Authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their plans and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those currently in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they plan to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

Fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his plans.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.
