#8247. CDT Southern Terminus Closure Lifted, Border Monument To Be Relocated

The Continental Divide Trail’s southern terminus and southernmost mile have reopened following a temporary construction closure, according to the Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC). This section of the trail had been closed in late October so that construction crews could widen an access road and construct a second border barrier at the terminus.

The first mile of the CDT falls within the Fort Huachuca New Mexico National Defense Area (NDA), a military zone created in spring 2025 when roughly 110,000 acres along the US-Mexico border were transferred from the Bureau of Land Management into Army control. Hikers seeking to access the trail’s southern terminus must submit to a background check and obtain an Army permit. Noncitizens must also have a US citizen escort through the NDA who also has an access permit.

“These events are unprecedented in the history of our trail system: the transfer of a critically significant element of our national scenic trail into the Department of Defense control, the conversion of the CDT Southern Terminus into a military and construction zone of momentous scale, and trail management partnerships that include land management agencies and state governments, but also the US military,” the CDTC said in a press release.

The CDTC received word today from US Army officials at Fort Huachuca that the trail is once again officially open, although construction activities are ongoing and hikers may still encounter traffic, road closures, and delays in the area. “This closure came at a critical time for southbound hikers,” the organization said. “Completing the 3,100-mile trail is a monumental achievement, and the construction activities at the border created dynamic changes to the permitted NDA access in place during the past year.”

The press release also indicates that the construction of the second border wall means the southern terminus monument will need to be relocated to an area outside of the border walls, and that access to the monument may be temporarily prohibited during construction and relocation. “CDTC does not know the exact timing of the relocation but will provide updates as available,” the organization wrote.

#8244. Young Climbers Bag New Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

An energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu. Eric Bazon, Pierre Girot, Sophie Jacob, and Kilian Moni did two new routes, including a first ascent of a 5,205m rocky spire and one very difficult line. They then climbed another peak on a “rest” day.

As soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition. Their acclimatization was also progressing more slowly than expected. Instead, they focused their attention on a ridge they saw from their base camp every morning. On October 20, Bazon, Jacob, and Girot set off toward the summit, while Moni waited for them at the base.

“Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote. The climb took three days on the ridge, bivvies included, and led Bazon, Sophie Jacob, and Pierre Girot to the west summit of ChekiGo (6,128m). It took another full day and one more bivouac to reach base camp.

Cheki Go’s main summit was first climbed in 2005 by Bruce Normand of the UK and Oliver Von Rotz of Switzerland via the west face. A Spanish team led by Mikel Zabalza first reached the west summit via a direct route up the west face in 2017. The team had just returned from bagging the first ascent of Jugal II.

“It was quite an intense experience for a ‘secondary’ project: one that combined rock climbing on mediocre granite, improvised protection, and steep snow ridges, all while hauling our ropes on our backs,” said Bazon.

The ridge was technical enough to be a good start: 5c on rock and M4 on mixed terrain. In Alpine grades, the team assessed it as TD (very difficult).

Since the weather forecast looked good for another four days, the team decided to continue climbing. They split into two teams: Bazon and Girot headed for a peak previously climbed by elite American alpinists Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey in 2014: Chukyima Go (6,259m). Like their predecessors, the French team approached the west face from the Naa Valley in Rolwaling.

“There was this direct, narrow, and obvious couloir that simply begged to be climbed,” Bazon reported.

The climbers at an open bivy. Photo: Eric Bazon

The next morning, they found the west face in great condition, which allowed them to climb a direct route to the summit along rock cracks, steep ice, and varied mixed terrain.

It took them two days (October 27-28), with one cold bivy on the face with their feet in their backpacks, to complete the route’s 23 pitches. Their West Face Direct route is 900m long, and the team assessed it as ED (extremely difficult), with M6 on mixed sections, and an Alpine ice grade of AI5.

The photo below shows that the new French route, TchikitaMa Go, runs to the right of the previous line opened by the two Americans.

Left: the new route opened by the French team, compared, right, to the 2014 line by Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey. Photo: Eric Bazon/PlanetMountain

Meanwhile, Sophie Jacob and Kilian Moni went for an unclimbed peak that also rose right in front of their base camp: 5,205m Janjmu. The pair completed the first ascent on an aesthetic 600m line up the north face. They called the route The Eternal Stars (“Les etoiles eternelles”) after some friends who had recently perished.

“It felt just like being at home in the Alps, with the added challenge of high altitude,” the climbers reported. “We pushed ourselves to the limit, both physically and mentally, across demanding yet incredibly logical pitches.”

But this was still not enough for the pair. They squeezed in a final climb of Yalung Ri in what they called “a contemplative, active recovery” day. They then finished the trip by paragliding from the summit.

Kilian Moni flies from the top of Yalung Ri. Photo: Kilian Moni

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

#8243. ‘8 Different Hunters Had Been After It.’ Giant Nontypical Buck Taken in Indiana

Published Nov 10, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Joe Merritt, age 41, of Middletown, Indiana had some target bucks he was after the first week of November during the state archery deer season. This is the first year he had cell cameras out to monitor multiple areas, and they proved to be a critical tool for taking the buck of a lifetime.

“On Tuesday, November 3 I got a trail camera photo of a huge buck sent to my cell phone from a very small woodlot that was my least favorite place I had to hunt,” Merritt tells Outdoor Life (he did the interview after just spending a morning hunting rabbits with his beagles). “The photos were of a huge buck that I’d never seen anywhere before.”

The next day the same cell phone camera got photos of the buck again. And the next morning, Nov. 5 at 3:55 a.m. he got photos of the huge buck again from the same camera in the same small wooded area.

“I knew I had to go after that buck right then,” says Merritt, who owns a coffee distribution company. “I left immediately and was in my saddle hanging from a  thin tree well before dawn.”

Merritt listened to deer in the woods around him long before daybreak. He wanted to be in his stand early to not disturb deer. He believes the spot was a bedding area near a sanctuary of private property where no hunting is allowed.

As an overcast dawn broke, he had a small 8-point buck come by his stand. Almost an hour later a doe showed.

“She kept looking behind her as she moved my way,” says Merritt. “She kept coming to me and flopped down and bedded just 35 yards away. The whole time she was looking back, and I was a little puzzled until the giant buck I had on camera showed up.”

But the giant buck moved toward the doe and bedded down near her, just 37 yards away.

“That’s when the chess game began,” says Merritt, who is also a dedicated houndsman who’s pursued raccoons and bears with dogs. “I was hanging from a very small diameter tree, and both deer were bedded close, and there was no chance for a bow shot while they were lying down.”

Merritt sat in his stand, quiet and still, for four hours before the doe finally got restless, stood, and walked toward Merritt. She was feeding on browse as she moved his way.

“That’s when the buck stood up, and started following her,” Merritt says. “The doe was right underneath me watching back at the buck when he turned and gave me a full broadside shot at 22 yards.”

Merritt made a perfect shot on the biggest deer of his life.

“I saw him running and blood was blowing out everywhere,” said the bowhunter. “I didn’t see or hear him fall. But I knew the shot was perfect and the buck would be easy to find.”

The doe was still feeding under his stand after Merritt shot and the buck ran.

“I just broke down in the stand, shaking and talking to myself about what just happened,” he says. “It took about 10 minutes for me to de-escalate and comprehend what had just happened.”

Then he climbed down to the ground and walked to where he’d last seen the buck. He walked right to the downed animal that was only 60 yards from where his arrow had struck it.

“I walked up to him and placed my hands on his rack and thanked the Lord for what had just happened,” says Merritt. “Then I phoned my wife and friends.”

Shortly, his close pal Jared Leppink joined Merritt in the woods and the two of them loaded the buck into an UTV. Then they shot photos of it, dressed the deer, and caped it.

While the buck has a massive rack, Merritt said the deer only weighed about 200 pounds – not a big animal for east-central Indiana, which regularly gives up 250 to 300-pound whitetails.

“I don’t think the buck was that old,” Merritt says. “The teeth were not very worn. I think he was between 3.5 to 5.5 years old.”

When pictures of his buck hit social media it created a wave of folks contacting him.

Read Next: Indiana Is Now the Top Trophy Whitetail State. Here’s Why

“I had to turn off my phone for 24 hours,” he says. “About eight different hunters had been after that buck and showed me photos of it. Some had shed horns from the buck from prior years. We figured I shot my buck 12 miles away from one hunter who thanked me for shooting the deer.

“I asked him why he was thanking me. He said, ‘Well now I know you got him, and I don’t have to keep passing other good bucks waiting for the 23-pointer to show up.’”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8240. Cozy Bed to Selden Pass — John Muir Trail Day 15

After last night’s fabulous dinner, I expected to sleep like a baby.  And I did.  For a while.

Then a very disturbing event occurred, relating to my left wrist injury.  I woke up in the middle of the night and my thumb, index finger, third finger and fourth finger were completely and totally numb on my left hand, and the pinky was partially numb.

I hoped (fervently!) that this only meant I had slept on my injured wrist in a bad way.  The alternative would seem to be nerve damage of some kind.  Of the kind that says, “Get off the trail right away and see a doctor!!”

Gradually I managed to get feeling back.  As it slowly returned, I was cautiously relieved.  But I recognized that if the extreme numbness came back, then it was not a random misfortune, but something I really needed to worry about.  Aside from possible long-term damage, hiking with no feeling in my left hand was out of the question.

The other change overnight was temperature.  When I turned in, it was hot, even stuffy in my little cabin home, so I went to sleep with just my shirt on, with bare feet and bare legs.  There was no top sheet on the bed, just a sheet on the mattress and a blanket.  So, I slept between the sheet and the blanket.

Over the course of the night, it started to get ever chillier.  As the night went on, I added my little knit cap; then I added socks.  As it cooled further, I got out my sleeping bag liner and hopped in.  Finally, I got my puffy jacket and wrapped it around my legs and eventually that seemed to do the trick.  I was extremely resistant to pulling out my sleeping bag, I did not want to do that if I could help it.  Somehow that would have made the overnight feel less like a true break from the trail, I guess.

When I got up in the morning, my fingers all still had sensation, they were moving.  My wrist was still injured, but my fear of nerve damage abated.

I went up to breakfast and oh what a spread!  This is a place that serves hikers. They had scrapple, bacon, pancakes, eggs, fruit, yogurt, and coffee, of course.  The same crew from the night before all sat around and we stuffed our faces, understandably, as hungry hikers are prone to do.

Smiles showed me a picture of the inside of her cabin from the night before and it was hilarious!

With a great fear of SPIDERS, Smiles had set up and slept in her tent INSIDE her MTR cabin!

This picture gives a good sense of how she obtained her trail name!

So that’s what retired New York oncologists look like!

Lauralyn was there too, and she said, ”You know, you said you were going to recite that poem, how about it?”

Lauralyn encouraging me to recite The Raven

I warned them all it would take more than ten minutes and they said, “That’s okay, go ahead.”

As everyone was getting served, and kitchen staff were moving through the room, I recited The Raven.  They said they really enjoyed it, and I think they did.  With the distractions in the room, it was probably not my best performance, but I did all right.

It was time to get going, so I got my resupply bucket that was stashed in the kitchen under lock and key for bear protection.  Shlepping it to my cabin it felt very heavy.  Then I opened it and there was so much stuff I didn’t need.  I began sorting – everything I wanted went on the bed for packing, everything I did not went back in the bucket.

Smiles dropped by and told me, “I extended, I’m gonna stay here another day.”

“Okay, fine,” I replied, adding, “you know, I’m so tempted to go up to the dining area and fill one of my water bottles with their lemonade!”

She said, “Come on, I’m going that way anyway, let’s go.”

Together we went up.  Maybe my plan was perfectly acceptable, but it helped to have a partner in crime.  I filled up on lemonade, and it proved so delicious on the trail, I enjoyed it so much.

While near the dining room I used the flush toilet, the only one on their whole property.  It didn’t seem like a big deal, but I wanted to get my money’s worth.  (It was $375 a night, remember?)

Unfortunately, I never went in the hot spring, and the people who believe in those things were just raving about it.  The day before, when I might have done it, they had girls cleaning it with toothbrushes and I just didn’t feel like it any other time.

Back in the cabin, I finished packing, surprised that almost all my food fit in the bear canister.  It seemed I was getting a bit more efficient at that task.  My charger block almost got fully charged, finally, so that was good news too.

Before leaving Muir Trail Ranch, I dropped off my plastic five-gallon  bucket full of not-needed items (mostly food) at the reception location.   Just at that moment a German couple arrived and said, “Oh we forgot to send food, we have no food.”

I replied, “Well this is your lucky day, there’s a ton of food in here.  It’s good, expensive food too.”  It was, because a lot of it was the pricey freeze-dried stuff.  Somehow, I had badly miscalculated.  Whatever the reason, that couple made out like bandits.  The adage, “the trail provides” was certainly true for them that day!

I was facing a long uphill, over 3,000 feet to cross Selden Pass, and the very first stretch was one of the steepest.  After a break, when you first start walking, especially uphill, and when your pack is heavy from resupply, your legs can feel like lead.  Mine felt that way, for sure, but the good news was, it didn’t last long.

Pretty soon I was going up at a good pace, but I was stuck behind a horse being ridden by next-door-cabin Jay, who was behind a horse ridden by his guide.  Oddly, my pace was pretty close to that of the horses, but I didn’t want to get in front and hold them up.  At the same time, walking behind I was breathing the dust they were kicking up, so I kept having to drop back to get clear of that.

Finally, there was some separation between us.  The ascent included a lot of long switchbacks, so that the “crow fly” distance to MTR was not that great.  I could even still see it, just far, far beneath me now.  My blood was really pumping from all the uphill!

I was pleased at how I handled it.  True, it was at a lower elevation, but I thought at last I might be getting my trail legs.  Soon I crossed over some forests and meadows and was out of sight of the resort.  I spotted some wildflowers by the trail.

Perhaps it was the season, but I did not see the profusion of wildflowers on the JMT I have seen on other trails

In one of the meadows I was puzzled.  There was a path straight across, but someone had blocked it off.  As I skirted the glade, following the detour, I came across the team building the trail on more sustainable ground, to preserve the fragile meadow.   These folks do such an important job, making the trail better for all of us, and getting paid rather small salaries for doing it.  As always I stopped and thanked them profusely.  I wanted them to know that they and their work were deeply appreciated.

I came to the twin Sallie Keyes lakes.  As I arrived, I crossed some steppingstones over the exit creek and saw a beautiful snake swimming in the water; a garter snake, I think.  I even got its picture.

Right after this shot I watched the snake enter the water and swim away

Feeling hungry, I was tempted to have lunch there.  But then I looked at the map, and saw that the last lake before Selden Pass was called Heart Lake, because it’s shaped like a heart.

I thought, “That seems very appropriate. I will go to Heart Lake and have my lunch.”  At Muir Trail Ranch breakfasts they also lay out the fixings for making and packing a lunch.  I had prepared a sandwich and packed it into my Nalgene soaking container.  I also brought a fresh apple.

When I got to Heart Lake, I took off my shoes and socks, dunked my bare feet into the lake, and ate half of my sandwich.  Under the dry surface of the moss I was sitting on, the lower portion was very wet, meaning my shorts were quickly soaked.

The moss is where I sat and the water is where I swam

As I realized how wet my seat was, I also realized the thought of a swim was very attractive.  So, I took off my clothes, put on my water shoes, and walked into Heart Lake.  I plunged my whole body in, swam out my usual 10 yards, then swam back.  It refreshed me so much.  And yes, I was skinny dipping, except for my water shoes.

But nobody came by while I was swimming.  Afterwards I dried off a little bit and put my damp shorts back on.  Then I ate the rest of my sandwich and my apple and finished off the MTR lemonade.  It was so good.  I’d been drinking it all day, climbing and climbing.  Now it was gone.

A little hard to see, but those are the two upper lobes of the “heart” that names Heart Lake

Energized by food and swim, I continued on up to Selden Pass.  It was a little weird, because no one else was there.  Usually when you get to a pass, you are not alone.  It seems people get to a pass, and they often stay there for a while.  The are resting, or eating, or just enjoying the view and celebrating their accomplishment on top of the world.  Sam and I crossed Forrester Pass alone, but that day the weather was challenging, so nobody stayed up there.

On Selden Pass I was alone, and it was nice to be there by myself.  Then I started down, realizing it was now around 3.30 p.m., which meant my progress was faster than I expected.  That morning I envisioned arriving at closer to 5:00 p.m.  It seemed I was in better shape than I thought.

View north from Selden Pass, the lake is Marie Lake

Descending I was trying to balance going pretty fast, while also being careful to avoid another accident.  As I  proceeded down, I met a couple of women and, in the course of the discussion, one of them revealed their hike was a birthday trip.

So, I asked the birthday girl her name (Sydney) and I sang “Happy Birthday dear Sydney” to her.  That’s just what I do.

Further down I met a woman, an American of Korean origin, who was just finishing a (very late!) lunch at a stream.  She told me her trail name was Ninja Queen because she is allergic to UV light and therefore wears a ninja’s face mask and bright reflector sunglasses.

Just then another couple came going southbound and she too was Korean and was even carrying a Korean flag!   She said some Korean guys had a bunch of extra flags and offered  her one.  She felt patriotic and said, “Okay, sure!”

The guy she was with had the trail name Eminem.  It seemed they had met on trail and were just friends.  We took a selfie of the four of us meeting on the trail.

Papa George, Flag Girl, Eminem, and Ninja Queen hiking the High Sierra!

Such a random coincidence, right?  I said she should take “Flag Girl” as her trail name.  But it didn’t seem to really appeal to her.

I proceeded down and down and down, trying to make up as much distance as possible, so that tomorrow’s trip to VVR, Vermilion Valley Resort, is a relatively short one.  I did stop to refill my water at a stream crossing, and Ninja Queen passed me while I was there.  We exchanged greetings and found we both intended to overnight at VVR on the following day.

Finally, I got to the tent site that I was targeting.  To my disappointment, it appeared packed full.  I walked up to a tent to ask if there were any spots available nearby, and it was Sally!  The news about spaces was not hopeful, but I enjoyed stopping and chatting with her briefly.  That was very nice, especially when she said, “Yeah, all day I was asking, where is George? Where do you think George is?”

When I admitted I left MTR at 10:00 a.m. she went, “You left at 10 o’clock???”  Only then did I feel a little abashed at my late start.

That campsite was full, then the next campsite was full too.  The sun was getting lower and finally dropped behind the ridge.  It was still light enough to see, but it was quickly darkening.  Finally, the third place was empty!  I found a spot that seemed adequate in the fading light and set up camp.  I soaked and then ate an al pastor rice dish that was actually good, and I hid my bear cannister.  It was too dark by then to think about digging a cathole.

My faithful Big Agnes tent in the campsite near the river

Then I settled in for another night in the woods.

#8239. Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

Caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

The pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

With no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

“With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

The paddling portion went quickly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”

Using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

They also effectively halved the 480km trek by packrafting over two large lakes, including Nettilling, the world’s largest lake on an island. Yet there was no way to ease the final 160km slog into Iqaluit.

Postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

“It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they said.

McDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

“One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We quickly packed our boats and got on the water.”

In Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8238. The Gun Industry Is Divided Over Federal’s New High-Pressure 6.5 Creedmoor Ammo. Here’s Why

Published Nov 10, 2026 1:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Late last month Bergara became the first gun manufacturer to explicitly state Federal’s 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak ammo is not approved for use in its bolt-action rifles. This reverses earlier guidance that the new high-pressure cartridge technology was compatible with Bergara’s existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles.

The 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak, introduced this summer, has the same dimensions as a traditional brass 6.5 Creedmoor cartridge and was specifically designed by Federal Ammunition for use in existing 6.5 Creed rifles. It is not a new cartridge, but an improvement to an existing cartridge. This unusual dynamic is part of the regulatory and potential liability concerns currently vexing the gun industry.

Federal’s proprietary steel-alloy case technology contains higher pressures that drive bullets at faster speeds for better performance. Plus Peak operates at 80,000 psi, compared to about 62,000 to 65,000 psi for brass 6.5 Creed cartridges. This is possible because the Peak Alloy case material that Federal has developed is much stronger than brass. It acts as a containment vessel insulating the action and barrel from the extra pressure without inflicting extra stress on the rifle.

Related: They Built a Rifle Cartridge That Could Change Hunting and Shooting Forever

The ammunition has undergone substantial testing by Federal, a dozen gunmakers and component companies, the U.S. military (which has ordered 40 million cases), and other industry professionals.

And indeed, Bergara rifles were originally deemed “compatible” with this 6.5 Creed Plus Peak ammo, according to previous guidance from Federal and media coverage of the ammo’s launch in June. But on Oct. 29 Bergara announced that the new ammunition “is NOT approved for use in any Bergara rifle chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor.”

“These cartridge pressures haven’t been evaluated under SAAMI’s standard development process,” reads the statement, referring to the Sporting Arms and Ammunition Manufacturing Institute. “Ammunition operating outside SAAMI pressure standards for its caliber should not be used in any rifle unless Bergara formally confirms compatibility for that model.”

SAAMI sets the gun industry’s self-imposed guardrails with voluntary performance standards for firearms, ammunition, and suppressors. Bergara did not cite any incidents of catastrophic failures or injury related to shooting the new case technology through its rifles. (No one we spoke to for this story reported being aware of a catastrophic failure while testing the Plus Peak in existing 6.5 Creed rifles.)

Bergara announced in 2025 it would launch rifles in 7mm Backcountry, which debuted the same high-pressure cartridge technology as the Plus Peak. Various online distributors and retailers indicate Bergara’s HMR Pro and MG Lite models would be available in the 7BC, but the company doesn’t currently offer any rifles chambered in 7BC on its website. It’s unclear if any preproduction or production models were ever manufactured. Bergara declined to comment for this story.

In a June statement, SAAMI acknowledged the development of the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak and the creation of a working group — at Federal’s request — to evaluate the new case technology on “performance, pressure, testing, and interchangeability standards.”

SAAMI and its member companies are also discussing “the technical issues and opportunities presented by advanced cartridge case technologies and their interaction with existing firearms and suppressors.”

The organization stopped short of taking a position on the ammunition and instead urged hunters and shooters to contact their rifle’s manufacturer before shooting Federal’s 6.5 Creed Plus Peak.

“At this time, SAAMI’s guidance stays the same,” SAAMI’s senior director of technical affairs, Alan Serven, tells Outdoor Life. “As this is not a standardized cartridge, we can’t really say anything definitive about it, so we are directing folks to the manufacturer of their firearm. And we do caution that an answer from one manufacturer cannot be interpreted as a blanket statement … It’s on a case-by-case basis with each of the manufacturers and potentially down to model.”

On Nov. 5 the sporting-goods retailer Scheels sent an internal memo to its employees announcing any Plus Peak ammo should not be stocked on store floors or made available to customers.

“As of yesterday morning we have added a ‘DNS’ Do not Stock rating to all SKUs of Federal 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak ammunition,” reads the memo, obtained by Outdoor Life. “The Kinetic Group [Federal’s parent company], gun manufacturers and SAAMI are continuing to review this product. Once we have more information on their review and the stocking of the 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak, we will make a determination on how to proceed.”

Scheels has put all direct orders for Plus Peak on hold, according to the memo. The retailer also instructed its ammo and gun teams to accept any returns from customers and put any received Plus Peak “somewhere where we can ensure it will not make its way to the floor to be sold.” When Outdoor Life called a Scheels store asking about Plus Peak availability and the possibility of ordering any, the employee who answered the phone replied that no, this was not possible because “corporate put the kibosh on this until SAAMI figures out the safety and pressure issues.” The store policy affects all five SKUs of Plus Peak.

“Federal’s Peak Alloy case technology is the wave of the future for rifle ammunition,” Kinetic Group’s VP of marketing Jason Nash tells Outdoor Life, noting that Federal sought to work with as many rifle makers as possible in its development of high-pressure loads. “Over the past seven years Federal has manufactured millions of rounds in multiple cartridges and firearms. Federal has the utmost confidence in this new technology and its function in today’s firearms.”

Some gunmakers have confirmed to OL that all their existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles are compatible with Plus Peak and they have no safety concerns whatsoever. Others have remained quiet on the advisability of using Plus Peak in their 6.5 Creedmoor rifles. Bergara remains the only rifle maker who has publicly disallowed its use in its bolt-action rifles. (Break-action rifles from CVA, Bergara’s sister company, are also not approved for Plus Peak, according to Federal’s site.)

This about-face on the use of Plus Peak in Bergara rifles raises many more questions than it answers. For instance, is this hesitancy around the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak rooted in legitimate concerns of consumer safety? Or is it ultimately driven by the potential threat that some companies see to their bottom lines? Here’s what to know.

Although the conversations around Plus Peak in SAAMI’s working group are confidential, industry insiders are keyed into the crux of the issue. Here are two of the primary camps.

No one seems to be disputing the performance gains of the Plus Peak ammo. Instead, the debate is over how to standardize it.

“It definitely is an interesting idea what Federal is doing,” says one gun manufacturer who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “The industry itself is not politicking against it. The industry is not against new technology. We know and understand new products are what drive business. That’s not the issue. There’s probably some ammunition companies that are bitter or angry they didn’t think of it first, but that’s also neither here nor there.”

According to this source, the problem is the new technology currently puts too much onus on gunmakers without the opportunity to earn revenue. In fact, it poses a big expense for bigger manufacturers.

“For those of us who played by the rules and built guns to SAAMI’s standards, now we have an ammunition out there that’s outside that spec. And we’re at a conundrum to say, ‘Is it safe or not safe in our guns,’” says the gunmaker. “So one [option is] we have to go back and retest all our guns at an immense cost to verify those guns will pass these pressures.”

Some guns will inevitably pass, they say, but other guns may not. This could result in a laundry list of liability concerns in which gun companies must painstakingly note — online and in owners manuals — which rifle models are compatible and incompatible with Plus Peak.

The biggest fear is that a customer will get hurt. It’s also a bad look for any existing guns that don’t pass, given that it “may expose ‘weaknesses’ that don’t exist” in rifles that were built to spec for standard 6.5 Creed loads.

Another option for gunmakers is to simply not retest guns and not comment on (or in Bergara’s case, publicly come out against) the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak.

“It does kind of stand in the face of why we have SAAMI and why we self regulate,” says the source. “So it’s a legitimate concern. We won’t approve [Plus Peak] either. Will our guns pass it? Most likely. But we’re not chomping at the bit to go through all the testing to verify that. We have other things we need to worry about.”

The right way to have handled this new ammo technology, in this gunmaker’s mind, was to have rolled out a new cartridge that could have more easily received SAAMI approval and allowed gunmakers to collaborate on new rifle builds.

“We would have all happily engaged in a new caliber that did this, like the 7 Backcountry. We knew the pressures, and we could build a gun specifically to handle that caliber with those higher pressures. No problem. It’s the retro-fitting for everybody. Why should we go to a pile of work? Just build a new caliber. It’s a very cool technology. We’re all about that. We’re not dragging our feet because we’re old and crotchety. We’re trying to protect our business and this industry.”

In that scenario this ammunition wouldn’t be a 6.5 Creedmoor using Plus Peak technology — it would be a whole new cartridge called, for instance, the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak. Of course, this would require shooters to buy a new rifle.

“The difference is meaningful,” says Outdoor Life shooting editor John Snow of this hypothetical scenario. “And presumably, you’d have to have firearms marked with that new cartridge name in order to be in compliance with what SAAMI has deemed acceptable.”

Federal has treated the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak not as a new cartridge, but an improvement on existing 6.5 Creed ammo. The difference, again, is that it contains higher-than-SAAMI-approved pressures that drive bullets at higher velocities.

These souped-up loads give hunters and shooters the ability to get 6.5 PRC-like performance out of their existing 6.5 Creedmoor rifles.

To some, the nature of Plus Peak is so monumental that industry disruption is natural and even necessary.

“We are embracing high-pressure technology like Peak Alloy,” says Sean Murphy, director of sales and marketing for Proof Research (and an occasional OL contributor). “It’s a development similar to switching from black to smokeless powder.”

Some of the more nimble gunmakers, like Proof, have already tackled the testing they need to feel comfortable about giving customers approval to run the higher-pressure load in its guns. That’s because Proof predicts this high-pressure ammunition is going to be a major player in the future, and the company is working to develop barrel and rifle technology to complement it by maximizing accuracy and performance.

“Proof Research has extensively tested Federal Peak Alloy cases in multiple cartridges, including 6.5 Creedmoor and 7 Backcountry,” says Murphy. “In 6.5 Creedmoor alone, thousands of rounds have been fired through hunting, target, and semi-automatic precision rifles with no case failures or firearm damage. Additionally, many thousands of rounds have been fired by Proof with Peak Alloy 5.56 ammunition, also without issue … Chamber-bore obstruction testing across every Proof Research receiver design showed Peak Alloy cases outperforming equivalent brass cases, with a greater safety margin at 80,000 psi than brass cases at 60,000 psi.”

The Montana-based rifle maker is also one of the most advanced barrel makers in the country. It spent years developing its PXT barrel, which Proof says accomodates much higher pressures and velocities without shortening the barrel’s lifespan.

“During our PXT barrel testing and development, more than 10,000 rounds of 7 Backcountry were fired — including 5,000 and 3,500 on individual receivers — with no damage, and wear levels comparable to brass-cased ammunition,” says Murphy.

The company also issued an apparent rebuttal to Bergara’s announcement of Oct. 29 with posts to Instagram and Facebook that same day, declaring full support and formal endorsement of Peak Alloy cartridges in its rifles.

“We have tested all our rifles — and many from other manufacturers — extensively with the Plus Peak ammunition and it’s proven to be completely safe,” says Murphy.

As part of its development and testing of the Plus Peak, Federal worked with a dozen gunmakers and related businesses. Federal confirmed to American Rifleman this summer that certain rifles from five of those companies are compatible with Plus Peak: Christensen Arms, Weatherby, Seekins Precision, Geissele, and Nemo Arms. Federal matches guidance from SAAMI that hunters and shooters should contact their gunmaker to specify which models are approved.

“Our testing has shown 6.5 Creedmoor +Peak operates in a variety of 6.5 Creedmoor firearm platforms,” Federal advises in the Plus Peak guide on its website. “Refer to your rifle manufacturer for recommendations on compatibility with high-pressure ammunition.”

Christensen Arms echoes similar language on its website. However, all existing Christensen Arms rifles chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor are compatible with the Plus Peak ammo, a spokesperson confirmed to Outdoor Life. The additional seven brands who worked with Federal include Area 419, Forster Products, Proof Research, Pure Precision, Hill Country Rifles, Short Action Customs, and Springfield Armory.

SAAMI has good cause to be extra cautious, points out Snow, since it’s a voluntary organization. The gun industry has regulated itself for a century — the result of a handshake deal with the government after World War I — and would like to continue avoiding federal oversight “like that of the auto industry,” says Snow.

But one reason gunmakers may come out against Plus Peak in their rifles has nothing to do with safety, cost, or liability.

“It’s possible that companies could see poor accuracy with the Plus Peak ammo and not recommend it,” says another industry insider, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity. “High chamber pressures, especially with some barrels and rifling designs, can cause accuracy problems that aren’t safety issues.”

Federal has patented its high-pressure cartridge technology, which means other ammunition makers can’t leverage it without paying for the privilege.

“There are rival companies that would arguably like to see this new and innovative technology put into a box and shoved off to the side,” says Snow. “Because they don’t have the ability to capitalize on this trend currently, and it’s potentially bad for their business if Plus Peak succeeds.”

The Peak Alloy case technology used in the 6.5 Creed Plus Peak was pioneered in the relatively new 7mm Backcountry, which debuted in January 2025 and was rooted in development of high-pressure ammunition for the military.

When the 7mm Backcountry was introduced, we tested more of it than anyone (besides Federal’s engineers) by shooting every SKU and running it in a dozen rifles. Although the 7BC delivered on its promise of velocity and produced accuracy equivalent to factory ammo in other cartridges, we encountered one major problem with almost every rifle. After 40 to 120 rounds, the 7BC rifles developed very stiff primary and secondary extraction. It turned out this was a common issue for other testers and shooters, too.

This issue, ultimately, was rooted in the case dimensions of the cartridge — not poorly cut chambers, as some people have speculated. After receiving updated 7BC ammo and testing the new batches in rifles that were previously showing these issues, we’ve found that the extraction issues have been resolved.

Those initial extraction issues in the 7BC were — erroneously — interpreted as effects of the increased pressure of the cartridge on the guns themselves. That doesn’t appear to be the case. In reality, most rifles chambered in 7mm Backcountry aren’t constructed differently from similar models designed for brass-cased cartridges like the 6.5 Creed.

So in other words, concerns over pressure issues from the new cartridge materials from the 7mm Backcountry to the 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak appear largely unfounded.

The 7 Backcountry was accepted by SAAMI without the current speed bumps, in part, because it’s an entirely new cartridge. It required brand-new guns manufactured specifically for the cartridge. Gunmakers could either opt to produce a gun chambered in 7BC — or not. Federal’s choice to offer the Plus Peak in an existing cartridge was a different route, but a calculated one.

“The reason Federal went with the 6.5 Creedmoor is because the 6.5 Creed was introduced in 2007 and is only available in modern firearms that are of recent vintage,” says Snow. “So it is extraordinarily unlikely, I would almost say impossible, that we would see, for example, a Plus Peak .308 or .223 offered commercially. That’s because there are way too many actions and rifles of older vintages that cannot be vouched for.”

Serven could not provide a timeline on when SAAMI’s Plus Peak working group might disclose its findings.

“Our primary mission is safety, so we are proceeding with that in mind. That concern is the overriding factor,” says Serven. “So we are not in a hurry. The priority is that we get the right answer, not a fast answer.”

SAAMI’s acceptance of new cartridges standardizes the case and load across ammo makers. The organization’s blessing is not required for the sale and use of ammunition, and many niches of the hunting, shooting, and military world operate outside the bounds of SAAMI approval. This includes everyone from brands like Buffalo Bore Ammunition to wildcat cartridge developers to the federal government itself. It also means you can still get your hands on 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak.

Federal currently offers the Terminal Ascent Plus Peak for sale on its site at a limit of two boxes per customer. The four other loads are “currently unavailable.” Plenty of YouTubers have been able to get their hands on the ammo, and none we’ve seen have reported safety issues.

“The stakes are pretty consequential,” says Snow of how SAAMI decides to handle the Plus Peak ammo. “On the one hand, are we going to move with less friction and resistance into the era of high-pressure, high-performance cartridges? Or are there going to be speed bumps and other impediments put in place that effectively throttle or discourage the adoption of this new technology?”

Read Next: I Shot the First Elk With the New 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak Ammo. It’s an Undeniable Elk Hunting Cartridge

The push to adopt high-pressure rounds has come from the U.S. military, which has mandated it to maintain an advantage over “near peer” adversaries (such as Russia and China) on the battlefield. The military wants rifles capable of defeating newer body armor, and the way to do that is to drive bullets from existing guns at greater speeds.

“The government has been crystal clear about what they want and expect,” says Snow, “which is that high-pressure cartridges are happening and need to be here sooner rather than later.”

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

Tyler Freel is a Staff Writer for Outdoor Life. He lives in Fairbanks, Alaska and has been covering a variety of topics for OL for more than a decade. From backpack sheep hunting adventure stories to DIY tips to gear and gun reviews, he covers it all with a perspective that’s based in experience.

#8235. Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long new route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

This first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic issues. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to quickly find a different goal.

Meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

The team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us new hope,” Steadman recalled.

Off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman

On October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential new line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

Steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman

“In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”

Chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” said Steadman.

“We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart

“The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

Summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman

“The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman

“Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”

After some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:

Following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

[We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, big hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

Happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman

The team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

“It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman said. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

#8232. A Bowhunt for Caribou Along Alaska’s Famed Haul Road Is Even Tougher Than It Sounds

Published Nov 10, 2026 2:58 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

We had to be getting close. I picked my way through the rocks along the edge of the half-frozen creek, knowing that any minute I would intersect trails beaten into the snow by thousands of caribou hooves. But could we make it in time? We couldn’t see the trails as we hurried alongside the steep cut bank, although I knew they had to be right here somewhere. I climbed up a few feet to peek over the bank, only to see a hundred caribou about 50 yards away. They saw me too. The stalk was blown.

The hundreds of caribou that we had tried to ambush were now moving away. Though we could hear the grunting, snorting, and occasional clash of antlers just over the hill, they might as well have been a mile away. They flowed like water over the tundra.

All we could do was look for another group of caribou to stalk. Luckily this shouldn’t be much of a problem, as thousands of caribou were migrating through this snowy stretch of rolling hills and wide valleys at the northern edge of the Brooks Range, within the largest bowhunting-only area on the continent.

The Dalton Highway, or “Haul Road” as it is commonly referred to, could be considered an irreconcilable dichotomy. It’s where ambitious industry and true wilderness meet—and coexist. The 414-mile industrial road was constructed in 1974 to facilitate building the Trans-Alaska Pipeline and service the new oilfields in Prudhoe Bay. It provides the vital link that allows oil to flow all the way to the Port of Valdez to this day.

Although its primary function is still to service the pipeline and oil fields, the Haul Road was opened to the public in 1980 and has provided and created access to millions of acres of public land. The Dalton Highway Corridor Management Area extends five miles on either side of the road and stretches about 370 miles from the Yukon River north to Prudhoe Bay, in which only bowhunting for big game is allowed.

“This is going to be a long drive,” I told my dad and our videographer Tanner Denton as we loaded up our gear with the snow still falling.

With about 500 miles to go and six inches of wet snow on the ground, we had a challenging drive ahead. The Haul Road is not only the most remote highway in the U.S., but it also has a reputation for tough driving conditions. It’s been featured on shows like Ice Road Truckers, and most rental vehicle contracts explicitly forbid driving on it. Even travel guides suggest bringing not one, but two new spare tires. For decades, the road was all gravel, and although some sections are now paved, much of the pavement is honestly worse than the gravel. On the drive, you’ll encounter huge potholes, frost heaves, rocks slung into your windshield from passing big rigs, and a unique silty sludge that will coat your entire vehicle. It was early October, and we knew that wet, muddy, and icy conditions were going to be a fact of life.

Despite the relatively easy access, popularity, and long seasons, I hadn’t ever really given an honest effort to a Haul Road hunt. I’m usually distracted by sheep and moose hunting, and aside from sneaking away on days off while working in Prudhoe Bay a couple times, the last time I had made the drive was in 2009 with my dad. So it was fitting that Dad was coming along with me on this trip.

Even so, this was anything but a slam dunk. As migrators, caribou are where they are, and you find them when you find them.

We hit the road shortly after first light. By the time the sun began to set, we were looking at more than a thousand caribou scattered across the barren hillsides in the northern foothills of the Brooks Range. With the temperature dropping quickly, it was time to set up camp, string our bows, and heat the wood stove. As we discussed our plan for the following morning, we hoped that the caribou tracks that littered the fresh snow around our camp were a good sign. I had been told by folks who are much more experienced than I, that this time of year, the herds of caribou will overnight up in the hills, then begin moving down in mid-morning. It looked like we were in a good position.

The next morning, we began gearing up as the coffee percolator thumped on the small wood stove. We periodically peeked outside the tent, looking for any major movement in the herds of caribou.

Our basic strategy was simple and dictated almost entirely by the terrain and the nature of the caribou. In herds of hundreds or more, on completely barren tundra, it would be all but impossible to sneak close enough for a shot with our recurves. When caribou did pass by terrain features that might allow a stalk, the herds were almost constantly moving. At a feeding, strolling pace, it would be impossible for us to keep up or gain ground on them to get into position. Instead, this hunt had to be an ambush. We had to take advantage of any terrain feature we could hide in, and let the caribou come to us.

“They’re pointed this direction,” I said as I stuck my head out of the tent. “I think we need to get moving.”

A herd of caribou was on its feet and moving on a low ridgeline about a mile away, angling for a ravine a few hundred yards from camp. Before we had much time to react, caribou began popping up onto the ridge on the other side of the creek, having already crossed. We had missed our opportunity.

“I think they’re going to drop down to the bottom eventually, so let’s work around and try to find a way to get in front of them,” I said.

We quickly hooked to our left, just above the base of the hills that the herd was moving along. They didn’t seem to be in a hurry. I don’t often think of caribou as an especially vocal animal, so it’s always surprising to hear their bellowing and snorting. As we crested the top of the hill which had been covered in caribou minutes earlier, we saw the last animals of the herd cresting over another skyline, headed farther back into the mountains. The barnyard-like scent of caribou hung in the air as we walked back.

When I saw the trails converge into one spot crossing the ravine above camp, I knew that this place had everything we needed for an ambush. The caribou had to cross a hilltop, then drop down a tall, steep bank, then cross two different channels before climbing out on a single trail that exited the other side. We would be able to see the next herd coming from camp, then quickly move into position to intercept them.

Back at camp, the percolator hadn’t even started boiling when another herd came over the far ridgeline, headed right for that creek. We threw on our backpacks and grabbed our bows, the herd moving closer with every precious second. The animals were coming from the north and I wanted to be on the south edge of the ravine. We would be able to hide and have plenty of time to see bulls coming and get ready. I didn’t cross the creek soon enough though, and it quickly turned to deep pools covered by unstable ice. Crossing now was too risky, so we continued moving upstream against the steep bank. Just as we had almost reached the trail that the caribou were headed toward, I looked over that cut bank and spookedthe entire herd. It was so close. If we had been just one or two minutes earlier, the outcome might have been different.

By that evening, the herds of caribou had abandoned their ridgetop route and began congregating in and moving through the valley below our camp. After rushing back and forth all day, we jumped in the truck and moved to a spot where we could see the entire valley. As evening began to fall, a big herd that had spent the day in the relative safety of the wide-open and flat valley began to move. Like spilled water trickling off a tabletop, a stream of caribou began to pull from the immense herd. In minutes, the line of caribou stretched as far as we could see into the mountains, crossing the creek just downhill of our camp. We tried one last time to slip into a gap in the herd, but that didn’t work either.

The next morning, we made the short drive from camp to where the road crested a nearby hill, giving us a good vantage of the whole valley. We could see hundreds (if not thousands) of caribou scattered across the foothills in the distance. They were beginning to move down to the valley floor. One cow would make the decision to go, followed by a single-file line of animals until the whole herd vanished. It was apparent that the whole mess of them was going to cross the road in a spot with virtually no cover and a howling 20 mph wind. To complicate matters, two other truckloads of hunters who were camped nearby were already positioning to try and have a crack at the approaching herd. We decided to wait where we were.

It was possible that some caribou could cross the creek we had been hunting, either above or below camp—we just needed to know which way they’d go.

As the caribou flowed across the road, we quickly turned around, parked the truck, and began walking down the creek to intercept them. They were crossing the gulley in a shallow, flat spot, several hundred yards from the edge of any brush. We managed to slip into a sizeable gap in the herd and were frantically trying to find a position to hide and wait, when my dad (who was kneeling right next to me) whispered, “There’s antlers right there, about 30 yards!”

If there’s one thing that’s a dead giveaway that a bull caribou is coming, it’s his set of tall antlers. If there’s any terrain between you, you’ll see his antlers long before he can see you.

If there’s one thing that’s a dead giveaway that a bull caribou is coming, it’s his set of tall antlers. If there’s any terrain between you, you’ll see his antlers long before he can see you. And at that moment, there were antlers sticking up above the small embankment—very close. We were in a bad spot though. I nocked an arrow, but Dad had to move away from me slightly. When he did that, the caribou spotted us and spooked, circling wide and crossing the shallow depression.

We cautiously stood and, not seeing any more caribou, tried to find a better position. Soon we spotted more antlers over a softly rolling rise in the tundra. Down on my knees, arrow nocked, I knew they were going to cross too far from us. In good conditions, 40 yards was pushing my reasonable limit with my recurve, but with a 20-mph wind, it was out of the question. One herd crossed at 75 yards, then another at 60, and then the herd fizzled out. After repositioning again and waiting, we decided to grab a cup of coffee and regroup. Each time we were getting closer, and we knew that something had to break our way sooner or later.

Before a much-needed lunch, I opted to drive back up to our vantage point and make sure nothing else was coming. Almost as soon as we got there, Dad and I saw yet another big herd. This group was on a trajectory that would take them near the line of tall brush that lined much of the creek, and we might have a place to hide. Again, we parked and hurried, walking through the brush as quickly as we could.

“We’re not going to make it in time,” I said, frustrated by our constant race against the clock.

I could see the backs of the caribou through the brush as they made their way across the open flat. They were just too fast, and we came to the end of the brush just as they started crossing the creek about 120 yards away.

“Why don’t you just try sneaking up there by yourself,” my dad said. “Three guys are too many, but one might be able to slip in there.”

It was worth a shot. Between us and the herd, the wash that the creek flowed through was about 3 to 4 feet deep, with a little bit of rolling terrain that might obscure the caribou that were coming. After a hundred or so had crossed, I began quickly, but carefully, moving down the draw. Eventually, some of the caribou that had already crossed began to see me, but kept on their way. I was still obscured from most of the animals that hadn’t yet crossed. I was skeptical about my chances, but after a small group saw me at about 60 yards, flared, and crossed farther down, a gap in the herd appeared. With antlers just coming into view, I quickly covered the remaining distance and dropped to my knees. I hid next to a small bush, arms-length from the main trail the herd had created. I watched the antlers, which looked to be following the group I had just bumped. There was nothing I could do but wait. I quickly ranged a rock in the cut bank across the winding trails in front of me. It was 30 yards away. I told myself I wouldn’t shoot at anything beyond that.

Seeing the rest of the herd safely across the creek must have calmed the caribou, because they quickly turned back toward me. All I could think as they closed the distance was: Don’t make eye contact.

Exposed, but holding absolutely still with my head tilted down, the cow that was leading the group came closer, followed by a nice bull. At under 10 yards I could hear her sniffing the air, even over the whipping wind. The bull was beyond her. As if I didn’t even exist, the cow walked past me, only paces away. My eyes shifted to the bull who was quartering to me, then to the rock I had ranged. He was only about 20-25 yards I figured, so I drew my bow.

I was in a state of calm disbelief. Somehow I accepted that, aside from the timing and placement of my arrow, the situation was totally out of my control. I expected the bull to come out of his skin as soon as I moved, but he didn’t even notice me until I hit full draw. His head turned toward me at some point, but I only remember checking off my shot process. Anchor, good alignment, aim, expand—and the arrow disappeared into the bull. I wanted to hit him through the meat of the front shoulder to fully catch both lungs, but my arrow went a little high and left. The bull crossed the creek in a sprint then turned back. I stood to watch him as he ran about 150 yards back to meet the confused herd. The second the bull stopped running, another big bull ran up, hooked his antlers, and threw my bull on the ground, thrashing him as if my bull owed him money.

After the herd moved off, I walked up to my bull, still in disbelief. This beautiful white-caped bull at my feet was the true embodiment of the Arctic. As a hunter, I always experience a sense of thankfulness and relief when I can finally put my hands on an animal that I’ve hunted, and I felt that with this bull.

But more than the thankfulness for possession, of meat, hide, antlers, there was something that I haven’t experienced so strongly in a long time. It was a raw appreciation of that moment, that every hunter feels right when it works out. The feeling transcends space and time and connects the hunter to the feeling of the arrow being released. That experience is a true gift that will last long after all the meat is gone.

Tyler Freel is a Staff Writer for Outdoor Life. He lives in Fairbanks, Alaska and has been covering a variety of topics for OL for more than a decade. From backpack sheep hunting adventure stories to DIY tips to gear and gun reviews, he covers it all with a perspective that’s based in experience.

#8231. The Slopeside Bubble

It may be November but it doesn’t feel like it. The day is warm and I treat myself to a late lunch at a resort. I run into a group of thru-hikers.

How would I fare on 4 hours of sleep? I was going to find out. In my determination to get the blog posts done yesterday I worked myself into a focused state and couldn’t fall asleep when I laid my head down. It didn’t help that I drove to the wrong trailhead last night, not my brightest moment. I remember it being close to 2:30AM when I was finally able to keep my eyes closed, and it was hardly past 6:00AM when I woke up.

The wet weather from the previous day had brought warmer temperatures, so it was easier to wake up and get ready for my final 2-day hiking stint of the week. Shortly after 7:00AM, I was heading north from the trailhead on Bake Oven Road.

Less than half a mile from the trailhead is Bake Oven Knob, a rocky section of the Blue Mountain ridge with amazing views of the valley below. Today it was overcast and a light rain fell as I approached the rocks. Patches of fog blanketed much of the land to the Northwest. To the South, it was more clear and there were a few openings in the clouds letting beams of light through. Below the rocks was a sea of reddish brown trees. It would be an amazing place to catch a sunrise. I pulled on my poncho and prepared to deal with miles of wet rocks, fun!

The Blue Mountain Ridge stretched on, and was fairly light on rocks. I made good time but felt a little let down by the views. I could see the valley through the trees, but there weren’t any open areas to get a clear view. I settled for partial views and remained thankful for the smooth trail conditions.

Interestingly, the trail crossed over a major highway, I-476, without the use of a bridge. The highway burrows straight through the mountain via a tunnel some 600+ feet below the trail. I stopped for a moment to see if I could detect any noise or vibrations permeating through the ground, but could only hear the sound of traffic before it entered the tunnel.

Low and high clouds along the trail today.

Further down the trail was the George W. Outerbridge Shelter, an older shelter but an important one as it has a piped spring directly on the trail. For a northbound thru-hiker it would be the last one for the next 20 miles. I’ve seen many comments on the road crossings about trail angles leaving water caches for hikers. I think they’ve probably stopped for the season by now, so I knew I’d either be making treks down the trail for water or coming up with an alternative.

Less than a mile down the trail from the shelter the trail crosses the Lehigh River on a road bridge. The river was almost perfectly still today, replicating the overcast sky perfectly. I looked at the north side of Lehigh Gap and saw the next stage of the trail was a steep rock scramble. The rain had stopped a while ago but it was intense enough to wet my wool socks. Those were then rubbing my ankles uncomfortably. At the far end of the bridge I decided to swap the wet socks out for my spares, something I hadn’t done since the day I climbed Katahdin. On that day, the difficult climb and high miles were enough to irritate my feet. I did learn that my other socks were much more comfortable, so I was looking forward to the incoming relief. I sat down, took the bag that has my extra socks and boxers out of my backpack, took my shoe off, and pulled off the wet sock. I turned to grab my fresh socks from the bag and saw they were no longer there. I was somewhat surprised, but I convinced myself that I must have removed them weeks ago to shed weight. An odd choice, but what other explanation could there be. I figured I’d just have to hike in the wool socks and probably end up with some gnarly blisters. I put the socks on and laced up my shoes. When I turned to put the bag back in my pack I saw that the fresh socks laying on the ground under my pack. They had popped out during my shuffling. With great relief, I went through the whole shoe removal process again. The ordeal reminded me of “losing” my tent straps for months when they were in the bag in my center console. I again managed to convince myself that I had lost something when in reality it was never far away.

Cozy feet were going to be essential for the rock scramble. While it was certainly steep, it was surprisingly short. I had to use my hands a few times but it looked far worse from below than it was. I do think it would be less fun to go down, so I planned to use the handy “winter trail” on my return journey to avoid the long step downs that have rattled my ankles a few times.

Looking up at the rock scramble north of Lehigh Gap.

Nothing like some fresh socks for ailing feet.

Looking north toward Weissport from Lehigh Gap.

Once I had cleared the rocks, the trail leveled off. A few rocky outcrops provided more valley views. I was hoping to avoid the 0.6 mile one way trek off the trail to collect water and noticed several commenters on FarOut pointing out that the Slopeside Pub and Grill, part of the Blue Mountain Resort, had a water spigot and was friendly to hikers. It was close to the trail, so after confirming it was open I figured I’d give it a shot. I strolled up after a few quick miles, during which time the day had gotten considerably nicer. It may have been early November, but it felt like late Spring. It was sunny and around 67 degrees. I decided I might as well have a bite to eat, it had been months since I last stopped for food on the trail. I walked into the resort and around to the pub. I was fully aware that  probably smelled a bit worse than the average resort guest. The first words out of my mouth to the hostesses were “Do you have outdoor seating?” I know my place. They showed me the way and I was even lucky enough to arrive during the lunch special featuring a bacon cheeseburger and fries for $10. Being a late spring day, it was only natural to pair the greasy fare with an adult beverage. The burger was served promptly and I sat back watching the other guests exploring the grounds. They seemed to be either early for a relatively formal event or maybe just surveying the locations. I might have felt out of place but I could practically see the AT from my table, this was as much my turf as theirs.

With my stomach full and my mind set on getting in another batch of miles, I left the resort via some maintenance roads and a short bushwhack back to the AT. I had topped off my water so I could at least make my breakfast in the morning. A short distance down the trail I turned a corner and saw a hiker building a fire. I had no trouble recognizing Rebar, the hiker I’d met last week at the Secret Shelter. I walked up and was pleased to hear that Pebbles and 2 other hikers, Greasetrap and Soaked, were on their way. Long distance hikers were starting to feel elusive, every time I ran into one they seemed to know several others that for one reason or another I hadn’t run into. We all chatted about the hiking in the area and being the most dense people on the trail – meaning we are the closest thing to a “bubble” on the AT. They are all planning a slack pack tomorrow with Mary Poppins, proprietor of the Breezy Acres hostel. I was tempted to join the group since socialization opportunities are few and far between these days but I had my mind set on getting in more miles.

Still battling the rocks, they never go away for long.

A well deserved and enjoyed afternoon meal.

Soaked, Greasetrap, Rebar, Pebbles, and See You Tomorrow chilling by the trail.

I stayed behind to make sure the fire we had going was dead out and then continued down the trail. I was hoping to accumulate more miles and make a dent in tomorrow’s mileage back to the van but by the time I reached the point I turned around yesterday it was going to be dark soon. Despite the lack of sleep, I only had one moment on trail where I felt sleepy. That changed suddenly when the thought of crawling into my tent first entered my mind. I also hoped to find a spot with an unobstructed view of either the sunset or tomorrow’s sunrise, but such views were few and far between on this section of the ridge. I found a decent spot nearby and made camp. It had been warm all day, but the temperature was dropping quickly. I passed on dinner since I still felt sated after clearing my plate back at the Slopeside Pub and Grill. I was asleep before 7:00PM, some 7 hours sooner than I’d managed the night before.

I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am new to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!
